questions.q: What is the electron configuration of Fe (Z = 26)?
questions.why: 26 electrons: [Ar] 4s² 3d⁶.

questions.q: Why is the first ionisation energy of oxygen lower than that of nitrogen?
o: The paired electrons in oxygen's 2p orbital repel each other
Oxygen's electron is in a higher shell
questions.why: Spin-pair repulsion in one 2p orbital makes that electron easier to remove.

questions.q: Which particle has 10 electrons and 11 protons?
questions.why: Sodium (Z = 11) that has lost one electron.

questions.q: Why does first ionisation energy generally increase across a period?
o: Shielding stays the same and nuclear charge increases
Nuclear charge increases, shielding is similar, so the outer electron is attracted more strongly
Electrons are added to new shells
questions.why: Examiners (2023): many said shielding 'remains constant'; examiners wanted similar shielding with greater nuclear charge and smaller radius.

questions.q: What is the full electronic configuration of Cu²⁺?
questions.why: Examiners (2023): answers often kept the 4s electrons. Transition metal ions lose 4s electrons first.

questions.q: Why does successive ionisation energy increase for every element?
o: Nuclear charge increases with each electron removed
Electrons are removed from increasingly positive ions with less electron–electron shielding
The number of protons in the nucleus increases
The principal quantum number of outer electrons increases
questions.why: The proton count stays constant while the electron cloud contracts, increasing electrostatic attraction per remaining electron.

long.q: Explain why the first ionisation energy of aluminium is lower than that of magnesium, and why that of sulfur is lower than that of phosphorus.
scheme: B1: Al's outer electron is in a 3p orbital, Mg's in 3s
B1: 3p is higher in energy / further from the nucleus / shielded by the 3s electrons, so easier to remove
B1: in S the electron removed is from a 3p orbital that holds a pair of electrons
B1: spin-pair repulsion makes it easier to remove

long.q: A beam containing protons, neutrons and electrons, all moving at the same speed, passes between two oppositely charged plates. Describe and explain how each type of particle behaves.
scheme: B1: neutrons pass straight through (undeflected) because they have no charge
B1: protons are deflected towards the negative plate
B1: electrons are deflected towards the positive plate
B1: electrons are deflected through a much larger angle than protons because their mass is much smaller (charges are equal in size)

long.q: The first six ionisation energies of element X, in kJ mol⁻¹, are 578, 1817, 2745, 11 577, 14 842 and 18 379. Deduce the group of the Periodic Table that X is in, explaining your reasoning, and write an equation, with state symbols, for the third ionisation energy of X.
scheme: B1: there is a large jump between the 3rd and 4th ionisation energies
B1: so the 4th electron comes from an inner shell, closer to the nucleus and less shielded; X has 3 outer electrons, so it is in Group 13
B1: X²⁺(g) → X³⁺(g) + e⁻

long.q: Write the full electronic configurations of a chromium atom (Z = 24) and of an Fe³⁺ ion (Z = 26), and describe the shapes of an s orbital and a p orbital.
scheme: B1: Cr: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d⁵ 4s¹
B1: Fe³⁺: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d⁵ (both 4s electrons and one 3d electron removed)
B1: an s orbital is spherical
B1: a p orbital is dumbbell-shaped (two lobes), with three p orbitals at right angles to each other

long.q: Explain why the radius of a sodium ion, Na⁺, is smaller than the radius of a sodium atom, but the radius of a chloride ion, Cl⁻, is larger than the radius of a chlorine atom.
scheme: B1: Na⁺ has lost its only 3s electron, so it has one fewer occupied shell
B1: the same nuclear charge (11 protons) attracts fewer electrons with less shielding, so they are pulled closer
B1: Cl⁻ has gained an electron into the same (third) shell with the same nuclear charge (17 protons)
B1: increased repulsion between the electrons makes the electron cloud spread out, so the ion is larger

questions.q: How many molecules are in 0.25 mol of CO₂? (L = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹)
A compound is 40.0% C, 6.7% H and 53.3% O by mass. What is its empirical formula?
What is the percentage yield if 8.0 g is made and 10.0 g was expected?
5.00 g of calcium carbonate (Mr 100) is completely decomposed by heating: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂. What volume of CO₂ is produced at room temperature and pressure? (molar gas volume 24.0 dm³ mol⁻¹)
questions.why: n(CaCO₃) = 5.00 ÷ 100 = 0.0500 mol, which gives 0.0500 mol CO₂ (1 : 1). Volume = 0.0500 × 24.0 = 1.20 dm³.

questions.q: 25.0 cm³ of aqueous NaOH is exactly neutralised by 20.0 cm³ of 0.150 mol dm⁻³ H₂SO₄. What is the concentration of the NaOH?
questions.why: n(H₂SO₄) = 0.0200 × 0.150 = 3.00 × 10⁻³ mol; 2NaOH + H₂SO₄ → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O, so n(NaOH) = 6.00 × 10⁻³ mol and c = 6.00 × 10⁻³ ÷ 0.0250 = 0.240 mol dm⁻³. Forgetting the 2 : 1 ratio gives 0.120.

long.q: 0.212 g of an anhydrous carbonate, M₂CO₃, reacts exactly with 20.0 cm³ of 0.200 mol dm⁻³ hydrochloric acid. Calculate the relative atomic mass of M and identify M.
scheme: M1: M₂CO₃ + 2HCl → 2MCl + H₂O + CO₂ (ratio 1 : 2)

long.q: Copper has two isotopes, ⁶³Cu and ⁶⁵Cu. Its relative atomic mass is 63.55. Taking the isotopic masses as 63.0 and 65.0, calculate the percentage abundance of each isotope.
A compound contains 54.5% carbon, 9.1% hydrogen and 36.4% oxygen by mass. Its relative molecular mass is 88. Calculate its empirical formula and its molecular formula.
scheme: A1: ratio 2 : 4 : 1, empirical formula C₂H₄O
M1: empirical formula mass = 44, and 88 ÷ 44 = 2
A1: molecular formula C₄H₈O₂

long.q: 4.86 g of magnesium is added to 100 cm³ of 2.00 mol dm⁻³ hydrochloric acid. Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂. Identify the limiting reagent and calculate the volume of hydrogen produced at room temperature and pressure (molar gas volume 24.0 dm³ mol⁻¹).
scheme: A1: HCl is limiting, because 0.200 mol Mg would need 0.400 mol HCl

long.q: 2.50 g of hydrated copper(II) sulfate, CuSO₄·xH₂O, is heated to constant mass, leaving 1.60 g of anhydrous CuSO₄. Calculate the value of x, and explain why the solid is heated to constant mass. (Ar: Cu 63.5, S 32.1, O 16.0, H 1.0)
scheme: M1: mass of water lost = 2.50 − 1.60 = 0.90 g
B1: heating to constant mass makes sure all the water of crystallisation has been driven off

questions.q: What is the shape of an ammonia molecule?
questions.why: Three bonding pairs and one lone pair: pyramidal, bond angle about 107°.

questions.q: What is the bond angle in methane?
questions.why: Four bonding pairs repel equally: tetrahedral, 109.5°.

questions.q: Why does water have an unusually high boiling point for its size?
questions.why: O–H…O hydrogen bonds are much stronger than other intermolecular forces.

questions.q: Which molecule is non-polar overall even though it has polar bonds?
questions.why: CO₂ is linear; the two bond dipoles cancel.

questions.q: Why does magnesium have a high melting point?
o: Strong metallic bonding: attraction between a lattice of positive ions and delocalised electrons
questions.why: Examiners (2023): some described the bonding in magnesium as ionic, and many omitted that the lattice is giant.

questions.q: What is the molecular geometry of sulfur hexafluoride (SF₆)?
questions.why: Six bonding pairs and zero lone pairs around the central sulfur atom repel equally into an octahedral arrangement.

long.q: Explain why water (Mr 18) has a much higher boiling point than hydrogen sulfide (Mr 34).
scheme: B1: water forms hydrogen bonds between molecules
B1: because O is much more electronegative than S (O–H strongly polar, lone pairs on O)
B1: hydrogen bonds need more energy to overcome than the van der Waals forces between H₂S molecules

long.q: State the shape of, and bond angle in, an ammonia molecule, NH₃, and a boron trifluoride molecule, BF₃. Explain why the bond angles are different.
scheme: B1: NH₃ trigonal pyramidal, bond angle about 107°
B1: BF₃ trigonal planar, bond angle 120°
B1: N has three bonding pairs and one lone pair; B has three bonding pairs and no lone pair
B1: the lone pair repels more strongly than bonding pairs, squeezing the N–H bonds closer together

long.q: Describe metallic bonding, and use it to explain why magnesium has a higher melting point than sodium.
scheme: B1: a lattice of positive metal ions in a 'sea' of delocalised electrons, held by electrostatic attraction between them
B1: Mg forms Mg²⁺ ions (higher charge, smaller) and gives two delocalised electrons per atom, Na only one
B1: so the attraction between ions and delocalised electrons is stronger in Mg and more energy is needed to overcome it

long.q: Describe how the σ bond and the π bond in the C=C bond of ethene are formed, and state the hybridisation of the carbon atoms.
scheme: B1: each carbon atom is sp² hybridised
B1: the σ bond forms by end-on (head-on) overlap of sp² orbitals, with electron density along the line between the nuclei
B1: the π bond forms by sideways overlap of the unhybridised p orbitals on each carbon
B1: the π electron density lies above and below the plane of the molecule (which prevents rotation about the C=C bond)

long.q: At low temperatures aluminium chloride vapour contains Al₂Cl₆ molecules. Explain how two AlCl₃ molecules join to form Al₂Cl₆, naming the type of bond formed.
scheme: B1: Al in AlCl₃ has only six electrons in its outer shell (an empty orbital; electron-deficient)
B1: a lone pair on a Cl atom of one AlCl₃ is donated into the empty orbital of the Al of the other (two such bridges form)
B1: this is a dative covalent (coordinate) bond

questions.q: Real gases behave most like ideal gases at…
questions.why: Molecules are far apart and fast, so their volume and attractions matter less.

questions.q: Using pV = nRT, what are the units of V?
questions.why: With p in Pa and R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, V must be in m³.

questions.q: Which assumption is made in the kinetic theory of an ideal gas?
o: The molecules take up a significant volume
There are no intermolecular forces between the molecules
The molecules are stationary between collisions
questions.why: Real gases behave least ideally at high pressure and low temperature, when these assumptions fail.

questions.q: 0.0200 mol of an ideal gas at 27 °C occupies 500 cm³. What is its pressure? (R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)
questions.why: Use SI units: T = 300 K and V = 5.00 × 10⁻⁴ m³, so p = nRT/V = (0.0200 × 8.31 × 300) ÷ 5.00 × 10⁻⁴ = 9.97 × 10⁴ Pa. The other answers come from using dm³, cm³ or °C.

questions.q: Iodine is a soft solid that sublimes on gentle warming, but silicon(IV) oxide melts at about 1700 °C. Which statement explains the difference?
o: The I–I covalent bond is weaker than the Si–O bond, so I₂ molecules break apart on warming
Iodine is a simple molecular lattice held by weak instantaneous dipole–induced dipole forces; SiO₂ is a giant covalent lattice of strong Si–O bonds
Iodine is ionic and silicon(IV) oxide is covalent
SiO₂ molecules are held together by hydrogen bonds
questions.why: Subliming iodine only overcomes weak forces between I₂ molecules (the I–I bonds stay intact); melting SiO₂ requires breaking many strong covalent bonds throughout the lattice.

long.q: Explain, in terms of structure and bonding, why aluminium conducts electricity and is malleable.
scheme: B1: giant metallic lattice of Al³⁺ ions surrounded by delocalised electrons
B1: the delocalised electrons are free to move through the lattice and carry charge when a potential difference is applied
B1: under a force, layers of ions can slide over one another
B1: the metallic bond is not broken because the delocalised electrons still hold the ions together (bonding is non-directional)

long.q: State two assumptions of the kinetic theory for an ideal gas. Explain why ammonia deviates more from ideal behaviour than nitrogen does, and state the conditions under which gases deviate most.
scheme: B1: gas molecules have negligible volume compared with the volume of the container
B1: there are no intermolecular forces between molecules (collisions are perfectly elastic)
B1: NH₃ forms hydrogen bonds between molecules, much stronger than the instantaneous dipole–induced dipole forces between N₂ molecules
B1: deviation is greatest at high pressure and low temperature (molecules close together and moving slowly)

long.q: Compare the structures of diamond and graphite, and use them to explain why graphite conducts electricity and can act as a lubricant but diamond cannot.
scheme: B1: diamond: each carbon covalently bonded to four others in a tetrahedral giant lattice
B1: graphite: each carbon covalently bonded to three others in flat hexagonal layers
B1: in graphite the fourth electron of each carbon is delocalised and can move along the layers to conduct; diamond has no delocalised electrons
B1: graphite's layers are held by weak forces (van der Waals) and slide over each other; diamond has strong covalent bonds in all directions

long.q: A gas has a density of 1.25 g dm⁻³ at 273 K and 101 kPa. Use pV = nRT (R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹) to calculate its relative molecular mass, and suggest the identity of the gas if its molecules are diatomic.
scheme: M1: take 1.00 dm³ = 1.00 × 10⁻³ m³ and p = 1.01 × 10⁵ Pa
B1: nitrogen, N₂ (or carbon monoxide, CO)

long.q: Carbon dioxide is a gas at room temperature but silicon dioxide melts at about 1700 °C. Explain this difference in terms of structure and bonding.
scheme: B1: CO₂ has a simple molecular structure
B1: only weak intermolecular forces (instantaneous dipole–induced dipole) between CO₂ molecules, so little energy is needed to separate them
B1: SiO₂ has a giant covalent (macromolecular) structure: each Si bonded to four O and each O to two Si
B1: melting needs many strong covalent bonds to be broken, which needs a lot of energy

questions.q: Hess's law is based on conservation of…
questions.why: The enthalpy change is independent of the route taken.

questions.q: 50.0 g of water rises by 6.0 °C. How much energy was transferred? (c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹)
Standard enthalpy change of combustion is always…
questions.why: Combustion releases energy, so it is exothermic.

questions.q: Which is the correct definition of standard enthalpy change of neutralisation?
o: The energy needed to neutralise an acid
The enthalpy change when one mole of acid reacts with one mole of base
The heat released when an acid is diluted
The enthalpy change when one mole of water is formed by an acid reacting with a base under standard conditions
questions.why: Examiners (2023): 'one mole of acid reacting with one mole of base' was a common inadequate answer, and some thought neutralisation needs energy.

questions.q: What is the standard enthalpy change of neutralisation between strong monoprotic acids and strong bases?
questions.why: Strong acids and bases dissociate completely, so the reaction is always H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l), yielding about −57 kJ mol⁻¹.

long.q: Use these standard enthalpy changes of combustion (kJ mol⁻¹) to calculate the standard enthalpy change of formation of propane, C₃H₈: C(s) −394, H₂(g) −286, C₃H₈(g) −2219.
scheme: M1: a correct Hess cycle or ΔHf = Σ ΔHc(reactants) − ΔHc(propane)

long.q: 50.0 cm³ of 1.00 mol dm⁻³ hydrochloric acid is mixed with 50.0 cm³ of 1.00 mol dm⁻³ sodium hydroxide. The temperature rises by 6.8 °C. Calculate the enthalpy change of neutralisation. Assume the solution has density 1.00 g cm⁻³ and specific heat capacity 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹.
scheme: M1: n(H₂O formed) = 0.0500 × 1.00 = 0.0500 mol, so divide q by 0.0500
A1: ΔH = −56.8 kJ mol⁻¹ (negative sign needed)

long.q: Use these average bond energies (kJ mol⁻¹) to calculate the enthalpy change for CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(g): C–H 410, O=O 496, C=O 805, O–H 460. Suggest one reason why your answer differs from the standard enthalpy change of combustion of methane, −890 kJ mol⁻¹.
scheme: M1: bonds broken = 4(410) + 2(496) = 2632 kJ
M1: bonds formed = 2(805) + 4(460) = 3450 kJ
B1: bond energies are averages from many compounds, or water is a liquid (not a gas) under standard conditions

long.q: Define the standard enthalpy change of formation, and write an equation, with state symbols, for the standard enthalpy change of formation of ethanol, C₂H₅OH.
scheme: B1: the enthalpy change when one mole of a compound is formed from its elements
B1: with all substances in their standard states under standard conditions (298 K and 101 kPa)
B1: 2C(s) + 3H₂(g) + ½O₂(g) → C₂H₅OH(l)

long.q: Use the standard enthalpy changes of formation (kJ mol⁻¹) Fe₂O₃(s) −824, CO(g) −111 and CO₂(g) −394 to calculate the enthalpy change for Fe₂O₃(s) + 3CO(g) → 2Fe(s) + 3CO₂(g). Explain why no value is needed for iron.
scheme: M1: ΔH = ΣΔHf(products) − ΣΔHf(reactants)
B1: Fe(s) is an element in its standard state, so its ΔHf is zero

questions.q: What is the oxidation number of Mn in KMnO₄?
questions.why: K +1, four O −2 each: Mn = +7.

questions.q: In Cl₂ + 2Br⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + Br₂, what is oxidised?
questions.why: Br⁻ loses electrons (oxidation number −1 → 0).

questions.q: What is the oxidation number of chromium in Cr₂O₇²⁻?
Cold dilute NaOH reacts with chlorine: Cl₂ + 2NaOH → NaCl + NaClO + H₂O. What happens to the chlorine?
o: It is only reduced, from 0 to −1
It is only oxidised, from 0 to +1
It is both oxidised to +1 and reduced to −1 (disproportionation)
Its oxidation number does not change
questions.why: One Cl atom goes from 0 to −1 in NaCl and the other from 0 to +1 in NaClO, so the same element is simultaneously oxidised and reduced.

questions.q: In acidic solution, MnO₄⁻ is reduced to Mn²⁺ while Fe²⁺ is oxidised to Fe³⁺. In the balanced equation, how many Fe²⁺ ions react with each MnO₄⁻ ion?
questions.why: Mn changes from +7 to +2, gaining 5 electrons; each Fe²⁺ loses only 1 electron, so 5 Fe²⁺ are needed: MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5Fe²⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O + 5Fe³⁺.

long.q: Deduce the oxidation number of: sulfur in Na₂S₂O₃; chromium in Cr₂O₇²⁻; nitrogen in NH₄⁺; manganese in MnO₄⁻.
scheme: B1: S in Na₂S₂O₃: +2
B1: Cr in Cr₂O₇²⁻: +6
B1: N in NH₄⁺: −3
B1: Mn in MnO₄⁻: +7

long.q: In acidic solution, manganate(VII) ions, MnO₄⁻, oxidise iron(II) ions to iron(III) ions and are reduced to Mn²⁺. Use changes in oxidation number to construct the balanced ionic equation.
scheme: B1: Mn goes from +7 to +2 (decrease of 5); Fe goes from +2 to +3 (increase of 1)
M1: so five Fe²⁺ react with each MnO₄⁻
A1: MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5Fe²⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 5Fe³⁺ + 4H₂O

long.q: Sulfur dioxide reacts with hydrogen sulfide: SO₂ + 2H₂S → 3S + 2H₂O. Give the oxidation number of sulfur in each sulfur-containing species, and identify the oxidising agent and the reducing agent, explaining your answer.
scheme: B1: S in SO₂ is +4
B1: S in H₂S is −2 and in S is 0
B1: SO₂ is the oxidising agent: its sulfur is reduced from +4 to 0 (gains electrons)
B1: H₂S is the reducing agent: its sulfur is oxidised from −2 to 0 (loses electrons)

long.q: Hydrogen peroxide decomposes: 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂. Use oxidation numbers to explain why this reaction is described as disproportionation.
scheme: B1: oxygen in H₂O₂ has oxidation number −1
B1: it becomes −2 in H₂O (reduced) and 0 in O₂ (oxidised)
B1: disproportionation: the same element is both oxidised and reduced in the same reaction

long.q: Write the half-equation for the reduction of dichromate(VI) ions to chromium(III) ions in acidic solution. Then, given Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ + e⁻, calculate the volume of 0.0200 mol dm⁻³ potassium dichromate(VI) that reacts exactly with 25.0 cm³ of 0.120 mol dm⁻³ iron(II) sulfate.
scheme: B1: Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 14H⁺ + 6e⁻ → 2Cr³⁺ + 7H₂O

questions.q: Adding a catalyst to an equilibrium…
o: makes equilibrium reached faster but doesn't move it
questions.why: A catalyst speeds up forward and reverse reactions equally.

questions.q: For an exothermic forward reaction, raising the temperature makes Kc…
questions.why: The equilibrium shifts to the endothermic (reverse) direction, so Kc falls.

questions.q: A Brønsted–Lowry acid is a…
questions.why: Acids donate H⁺; bases accept them.

questions.q: How does adding a catalyst affect the equilibrium constant Kc of a reversible reaction?
o: Kc increases because activation energy is lowered
Kc decreases because reactants are consumed faster
Kc is unchanged because forward and reverse rates increase equally
questions.why: A catalyst speeds up both forward and backward reactions by the same factor without altering the thermodynamic equilibrium position.

questions.q: For N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), what are the units of Kc?
questions.why: Kc = [NH₃]² ÷ ([N₂][H₂]³), so the units are (mol dm⁻³)² ÷ (mol dm⁻³)⁴ = (mol dm⁻³)⁻² = mol⁻² dm⁶.

long.q: 0.50 mol of H₂ and 0.50 mol of I₂ are heated in a sealed 1.00 dm³ flask until equilibrium: H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g). At equilibrium there are 0.78 mol of HI. Calculate Kc.
scheme: M1: H₂ and I₂ used = 0.39 mol each
M1: at equilibrium [H₂] = [I₂] = 0.11 mol dm⁻³
A1: Kc = 50 (no units)

long.q: In the Haber process, N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), ΔH = −92 kJ mol⁻¹. Explain the effect on the equilibrium yield of ammonia of increasing the pressure and of increasing the temperature, and explain why a temperature of about 450 °C is used.
scheme: B1: increasing pressure moves the equilibrium to the right, increasing the yield
B1: because there are fewer moles of gas on the right (2) than on the left (4)
B1: increasing temperature moves the equilibrium to the left, in the endothermic direction
B1: so the yield of ammonia decreases
B1: 450 °C is a compromise: a lower temperature gives a higher yield but the rate would be too slow

long.q: For 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g), write the expression for Kc. A 2.00 dm³ vessel at equilibrium contains 0.400 mol SO₂, 0.100 mol O₂ and 1.20 mol SO₃. Calculate Kc and give its units.
scheme: B1: Kc = [SO₃]² ÷ ([SO₂]²[O₂])
M1: concentrations: SO₂ 0.200, O₂ 0.0500, SO₃ 0.600 mol dm⁻³
B1: units dm³ mol⁻¹

long.q: Ethanoic acid reacts with water: CH₃COOH + H₂O ⇌ CH₃COO⁻ + H₃O⁺. Use Brønsted–Lowry theory to identify the two conjugate acid–base pairs, and explain why 0.10 mol dm⁻³ ethanoic acid has a higher pH than 0.10 mol dm⁻³ hydrochloric acid.
scheme: B1: an acid is a proton (H⁺) donor and a base is a proton acceptor; a conjugate pair differ by one H⁺
B1: CH₃COOH (acid) and CH₃COO⁻ (conjugate base)
B1: H₃O⁺ (acid) and H₂O (conjugate base)
B1: ethanoic acid is a weak acid and only partially dissociates, while HCl dissociates fully
B1: so [H⁺] is lower in the ethanoic acid and its pH is higher

long.q: State the features of a system in dynamic equilibrium, and explain why adding a catalyst does not change the position of the equilibrium.
scheme: B1: the rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the reverse reaction
B1: the concentrations of reactants and products stay constant
B1: it is in a closed system
B1: a catalyst increases the rates of the forward and reverse reactions equally, so equilibrium is reached faster but its position is unchanged

questions.q: On a Boltzmann distribution, raising the temperature…
o: moves the peak left and up
moves the peak right and down, with more molecules above Ea
reduces the area under the curve
questions.why: More molecules have energy at or above the activation energy; the total area stays the same.

questions.q: A catalyst works by…
o: providing an alternative route with a lower activation energy
questions.why: More particles then have enough energy to react.

questions.q: How does a catalyst increase the rate of reaction?
o: It increases the number of collisions
It increases the kinetic energy of the particles
It provides an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy, so more collisions are successful
It shifts the equilibrium to the right
questions.why: Examiners (2023): many said a catalyst increases the number of collisions rather than the frequency of successful collisions.

questions.q: For a first-order reaction with respect to reactant A, what is the effect on rate of tripling the concentration of A?
o: The rate increases by a factor of 9
questions.why: Rate = k[A]¹; doubling or tripling [A] changes the rate by that exact multiple for a first-order reaction.

questions.q: Marble chips react with excess dilute hydrochloric acid. Which change would NOT increase the initial rate of reaction?
o: Using powdered marble instead of chips
Using the same mass of marble as larger chips
Using acid of double the concentration
questions.why: Larger chips have a smaller total surface area, so there are fewer collisions per second between acid particles and the solid, and the rate decreases.

long.q: Use the Boltzmann distribution to explain why a small rise in temperature greatly increases the rate of a reaction.
scheme: B1: at higher temperature the curve shifts right / lower peak, area unchanged
B1: many more molecules have energy ≥ Ea
B1: so more frequent successful collisions per second (frequency of collisions rises only slightly)

long.q: Explain, with reference to the Boltzmann distribution, how a catalyst increases the rate of a reaction.
scheme: B1: the catalyst provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy
B1: on the Boltzmann distribution a greater proportion (area) of molecules have energy ≥ the lower Ea
B1: so there are more successful collisions per unit time

long.q: 0.50 g of calcium carbonate chips react with excess hydrochloric acid; 120 cm³ of carbon dioxide is collected in the first 60 s, after which the reaction has stopped. Calculate the average rate over the 60 s in cm³ s⁻¹ and in mol s⁻¹ (molar gas volume 24.0 dm³ mol⁻¹). Explain why the same mass of powdered calcium carbonate gives a faster initial rate but the same final volume of gas.
scheme: M1: rate = 120 ÷ 60 = 2.00 cm³ s⁻¹
B1: powder has a larger surface area, so more frequent collisions with acid particles
B1: the amount of CaCO₃ (the limiting reagent) is the same, so the same total amount of CO₂ forms

long.q: State what is meant by activation energy. A mixture of hydrogen and iodine gases is compressed into a smaller volume at constant temperature. Explain why the rate of reaction increases.
scheme: B1: activation energy is the minimum energy that colliding particles need in order to react
B1: compressing increases the number of molecules per unit volume (concentration)
B1: so collisions are more frequent
B1: the proportion of molecules with energy ≥ Ea is unchanged (same temperature), so the number of successful collisions per unit time rises

long.q: Describe how you could follow the rate of the reaction between magnesium ribbon and dilute hydrochloric acid, and how you would find the initial rate from your results.
scheme: B1: collect the hydrogen in a gas syringe (or measure the loss in mass on a balance)
B1: record the volume (or mass) at regular time intervals using a stopwatch
B1: plot volume of gas against time
B1: initial rate = gradient of the tangent to the curve at t = 0

questions.q: Across Period 3, atomic radius…
questions.why: Nuclear charge rises with similar shielding, pulling the electrons closer.

questions.q: Which Period 3 oxide is amphoteric?
questions.why: Al₂O₃ reacts with both acids and bases.

questions.q: Why does atomic radius decrease across Period 3?
o: Electrons are added to new shells
Nuclear charge increases while shielding stays similar
questions.why: Examiners (2023): say 'similar shielding', and link more protons to stronger attraction.

questions.q: Which Period 3 chloride dissolves in water to give a neutral solution of about pH 7?
questions.why: Ionic NaCl simply dissolves; AlCl₃ gives an acidic solution and the covalent chlorides SiCl₄ and PCl₅ are hydrolysed to give HCl (pH 1–2).

questions.q: Why is the melting point of silicon much higher than that of phosphorus?
o: Silicon atoms are smaller than phosphorus atoms
Silicon has metallic bonding with delocalised electrons
Phosphorus has fewer protons in its nucleus
Silicon is a giant covalent lattice, whereas phosphorus is made of P₄ molecules held by weak instantaneous dipole–induced dipole forces
questions.why: Melting silicon breaks many strong covalent bonds; melting phosphorus only overcomes weak intermolecular forces between P₄ molecules.

long.q: Explain the variation in melting point of the Period 3 elements from sodium to argon.
scheme: B1: Na to Al: metallic bonding gets stronger (more delocalised electrons per atom, higher charge and smaller ions), so melting point rises
B1: Si has the highest melting point: giant covalent structure with many strong covalent bonds to break
B1: P₄, S₈, Cl₂ and Ar are simple molecular (or atomic) with only weak instantaneous dipole–induced dipole forces, so low melting points
B1: S₈ > P₄ > Cl₂ > Ar because molecules with more electrons have stronger instantaneous dipole–induced dipole forces

long.q: Write equations for the reactions of sodium oxide and sulfur trioxide with water, giving the approximate pH of each solution. Explain, with equations, why aluminium oxide is described as amphoteric.
scheme: B1: Na₂O + H₂O → 2NaOH; pH about 13–14
B1: SO₃ + H₂O → H₂SO₄; pH about 0–1
B1: amphoteric: Al₂O₃ reacts with both acids and bases (it does not dissolve in water)
B1: Al₂O₃ + 6HCl → 2AlCl₃ + 3H₂O
B1: Al₂O₃ + 2NaOH + 3H₂O → 2NaAl(OH)₄

long.q: Sodium chloride and silicon tetrachloride are added separately to water. Describe what happens in each case, with an equation for any reaction, and give the approximate pH of each resulting solution.
scheme: B1: NaCl dissolves to give a neutral solution, pH 7 (ions are hydrated, no reaction with water)
B1: SiCl₄ reacts vigorously (hydrolysis), giving white fumes and a white solid
B1: SiCl₄ + 2H₂O → SiO₂ + 4HCl
B1: the solution is strongly acidic, pH about 1–2

long.q: Describe what you would see when sodium, magnesium and sulfur are each burned in oxygen, and write an equation for each reaction.
scheme: B1: sodium burns with a yellow/orange flame to form a white solid: 4Na + O₂ → 2Na₂O
B1: magnesium burns with a brilliant white flame to form a white solid: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO
B1: sulfur burns with a blue flame to form a colourless, choking gas: S + O₂ → SO₂

long.q: Give the formula of the highest oxide of each of the Period 3 elements Na, Mg, Al, Si, P and S, with the oxidation number of the Period 3 element in each. Explain the change in bonding across these oxides.
scheme: B1: Na₂O +1, MgO +2, Al₂O₃ +3
B1: SiO₂ +4, P₄O₁₀ +5, SO₃ +6
B1: the oxidation number equals the number of outer-shell electrons used in bonding
B1: bonding changes from ionic (Na₂O, MgO, Al₂O₃) to covalent (SiO₂ giant, P₄O₁₀ and SO₃ simple molecular) as the electronegativity difference from oxygen decreases

questions.q: Down Group 2, the solubility of the hydroxides…
questions.why: Mg(OH)₂ is sparingly soluble; Ba(OH)₂ is much more soluble.

questions.q: Down Group 2, the thermal stability of the carbonates…
questions.why: Larger cations polarise the carbonate ion less, so it is harder to decompose.

questions.q: How does the solubility of the Group 2 hydroxides change down the group?
questions.why: Mg(OH)₂ is sparingly soluble; Ba(OH)₂ is much more soluble. (Group 2 sulfates show the opposite trend.)

questions.q: Which equation shows the reaction of magnesium with steam?
questions.why: With steam magnesium forms its oxide and hydrogen; Mg(OH)₂ forms in the very slow reaction with cold water, and magnesium is +2, never +1.

questions.q: Why does the reactivity of the Group 2 metals with water increase down the group?
o: The nuclear charge decreases down the group
The sum of the first and second ionisation energies decreases, so M²⁺ ions form more easily
questions.why: Down the group the outer electrons are further from the nucleus and more shielded, so less energy is needed to remove two electrons, even though nuclear charge increases.

long.q: Describe the reactions of magnesium and of calcium with water, giving the conditions, what you would see, and an equation for each.
scheme: B1: magnesium reacts very slowly with cold water but burns with a white flame when heated in steam
B1: Mg + H₂O(g) → MgO + H₂
B1: calcium reacts steadily with cold water: fizzing, the metal disappears and the solution turns cloudy (white solid)
B1: Ca + 2H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ + H₂

long.q: Describe the trends in solubility of the Group 2 hydroxides and sulfates down the group. Describe how one of these trends is used to test for sulfate ions in solution, with an ionic equation.
scheme: B1: hydroxides become more soluble down the group
B1: sulfates become less soluble down the group
B1: add dilute acid (HCl or HNO₃) then aqueous barium chloride (or barium nitrate): a white precipitate forms
B1: Ba²⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq) → BaSO₄(s)

long.q: Write an equation for the thermal decomposition of calcium nitrate, and state the trend in thermal stability of the Group 2 carbonates down the group. Calculate the mass of calcium oxide formed when 5.00 g of calcium carbonate is completely decomposed. (Mr: CaCO₃ 100.1, CaO 56.1)
scheme: B1: 2Ca(NO₃)₂ → 2CaO + 4NO₂ + O₂
B1: thermal stability increases down the group (higher temperature needed to decompose)

long.q: Explain why farmers add calcium hydroxide to some soils, with an ionic equation, and suggest one advantage of using powdered calcium carbonate instead.
scheme: B1: to neutralise acidic soil (raise the pH) so that crops grow better
B1: OH⁻ + H⁺ → H₂O
B1: CaCO₃ is insoluble, so it acts slowly over a long time and does not make the soil too alkaline (CaCO₃ + 2H⁺ → Ca²⁺ + H₂O + CO₂)

long.q: Explain why the Group 2 metals become more reactive down the group.
scheme: B1: atomic radius increases down the group (more electron shells)
B1: more shielding by inner electrons outweighs the greater nuclear charge, so the outer electrons are attracted less strongly
B1: so the first and second ionisation energies decrease and M²⁺ ions form more easily

questions.q: Concentrated H₂SO₄ is added to solid NaBr. Which is produced?
o: HBr and some Br₂ and SO₂
questions.why: Bromide is a strong enough reducing agent to reduce some of the sulfuric acid to SO₂.

questions.q: Silver nitrate gives a cream precipitate soluble in concentrated ammonia. Which halide?
questions.why: AgCl is white (dissolves in dilute NH₃), AgBr cream (concentrated), AgI yellow (insoluble).

questions.q: Which reagent is used to test for halide ions (X⁻), as opposed to a halogen (X₂)?
questions.why: Examiners (2023): some used iodine where iodide was meant: be precise about halogens (X₂) and halides (X⁻). Halide ions are tested with aqueous silver nitrate.

questions.q: Chlorine water is added to colourless aqueous potassium iodide. What is observed?
o: No change, because chlorine is less reactive than iodine
The solution turns brown as iodine forms
questions.why: Chlorine is the stronger oxidising agent: Cl₂ + 2I⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + I₂, and aqueous iodine is brown.

questions.q: Why does the volatility of the halogens decrease from chlorine to iodine?
o: The molecules have more electrons, so instantaneous dipole–induced dipole forces between them are stronger
The X–X covalent bond becomes stronger
Hydrogen bonding increases down the group
questions.why: Boiling a halogen only overcomes intermolecular forces; larger molecules with more electrons have stronger id–id forces, so more energy is needed.

long.q: Give the colour and physical state at room temperature of chlorine, bromine and iodine, and explain the trend in their volatility down the group.
scheme: B1: chlorine is a pale green (yellow-green) gas and bromine is a red-brown liquid
B1: iodine is a grey-black solid (purple vapour)
B1: volatility decreases down the group
B1: larger molecules with more electrons have stronger instantaneous dipole–induced dipole forces, which need more energy to overcome

long.q: Chlorine water is added to aqueous potassium bromide. Describe what you would see, write the ionic equation, and explain the reaction in terms of the oxidising power of the halogens.
scheme: B1: the colourless solution turns orange (yellow-orange)
B1: Cl₂ + 2Br⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + Br₂
B1: chlorine is a stronger oxidising agent than bromine: Cl is smaller, so it attracts an incoming electron more strongly, and it oxidises Br⁻

long.q: Describe how aqueous silver nitrate followed by aqueous ammonia can be used to distinguish between separate solutions of sodium chloride, sodium bromide and sodium iodide.
scheme: B1: acidify with dilute nitric acid, then add aqueous silver nitrate
B1: chloride: white precipitate, which dissolves in dilute ammonia
B1: bromide: cream precipitate, which dissolves in concentrated (not dilute) ammonia
B1: iodide: yellow precipitate, which does not dissolve even in concentrated ammonia
B1: Ag⁺(aq) + X⁻(aq) → AgX(s)

long.q: Describe and explain the difference between the reactions of concentrated sulfuric acid with solid sodium chloride and with solid sodium iodide.
scheme: B1: with NaCl: steamy white fumes of hydrogen chloride
B1: NaCl + H₂SO₄ → NaHSO₄ + HCl, an acid–base reaction, not redox
B1: with NaI: purple vapour / black solid (iodine), plus a smell of bad eggs (H₂S) or yellow solid (S)
B1: I⁻ is oxidised to I₂ and the sulfuric acid is reduced (to SO₂, S or H₂S)
B1: I⁻ is a much stronger reducing agent than Cl⁻ because it is larger, so it loses an electron more easily

long.q: Chlorine reacts with hot concentrated aqueous sodium hydroxide. Write the equation, give the oxidation numbers of chlorine involved, and name the chlorine-containing product other than sodium chloride. State why chlorine is added to drinking water.
scheme: B1: 3Cl₂ + 6NaOH → 5NaCl + NaClO₃ + 3H₂O
B1: chlorine goes from 0 to −1 (in NaCl) and +5 (in NaClO₃): disproportionation
B1: sodium chlorate(V)
B1: to kill bacteria (Cl₂ + H₂O → HCl + HClO; HClO is the active disinfectant)

questions.q: Why is N₂ unreactive?
o: Its triple bond is very strong
questions.why: N≡N has a high bond energy.

questions.q: Which pollutant forms when nitrogen and oxygen react in a hot engine?
questions.why: High temperatures let N₂ and O₂ combine to form nitrogen oxides.

questions.q: Why is nitrogen gas very unreactive?
o: The N≡N triple bond has a very high bond energy
questions.why: A lot of energy is needed to break the triple bond, and the molecule is non-polar.

questions.q: In polluted air, NO₂ helps convert SO₂ into SO₃: SO₂ + NO₂ → SO₃ + NO, then NO + ½O₂ → NO₂. What is the role of NO₂?
o: It is a reducing agent that is used up
It is a catalyst: it oxidises SO₂ and is then regenerated
It is a product of acid rain
It reacts with SO₂ to form sulfuric acid directly
questions.why: NO₂ takes part in the first step and is reformed in the second, so it is not used up overall: it acts as a catalyst for the oxidation of SO₂.

questions.q: Which test confirms that a solid contains ammonium ions?
o: Add dilute HCl; a gas turns limewater milky
Add aqueous silver nitrate; a white precipitate forms
Warm with aqueous NaOH; a gas turns damp red litmus blue
Add acidified barium chloride; a white precipitate forms
questions.why: OH⁻ removes a proton from NH₄⁺: NH₄⁺ + OH⁻ → NH₃ + H₂O, and ammonia is the only common alkaline gas.

long.q: Explain why nitrogen gas is very unreactive.
scheme: B1: the two N atoms are joined by a triple bond (N≡N)
B1: the bond energy is very high, so the activation energy of reactions is very high
B1: the molecule is non-polar, so it does not attract electrophiles or nucleophiles

long.q: Explain, with an equation, how ammonia acts as a Brønsted–Lowry base. Describe how the bond formed arises, and state the shape and bond angle of the ion produced.
scheme: B1: NH₃ + H⁺ → NH₄⁺; ammonia accepts a proton
B1: the lone pair on nitrogen forms a dative covalent bond to H⁺
B1: NH₄⁺ is tetrahedral
B1: bond angle 109.5° (four bonding pairs repel equally, no lone pair)

long.q: Describe how you would show that a white solid contains ammonium ions, including an ionic equation.
scheme: B1: warm the solid with aqueous sodium hydroxide
B1: the gas given off turns damp red litmus paper blue (ammonia)
B1: NH₄⁺ + OH⁻ → NH₃ + H₂O

long.q: Explain how nitrogen monoxide forms in a car engine, and how it is removed by a catalytic converter. Give an equation for each process.
scheme: B1: the very high temperature in the engine provides enough energy to break the N≡N bond
B1: N₂ + O₂ → 2NO
B1: in the catalytic converter NO reacts with carbon monoxide on a platinum/rhodium surface
B1: 2CO + 2NO → 2CO₂ + N₂

long.q: Nitrogen dioxide in the atmosphere acts as a catalyst in the oxidation of sulfur dioxide. Explain this with equations, and state one environmental consequence.
scheme: B1: SO₂ + NO₂ → SO₃ + NO
B1: NO + ½O₂ → NO₂
B1: NO₂ is regenerated, so it is a catalyst (overall SO₂ + ½O₂ → SO₃)
B1: SO₃ + H₂O → H₂SO₄ gives acid rain, which damages limestone buildings, trees or aquatic life

questions.q: Structural isomers have the same…
questions.why: Same molecular formula, different structures.

questions.q: Why can but-2-ene show cis/trans (E/Z) isomerism?
o: There is restricted rotation about C=C with two different groups on each carbon
questions.why: Both conditions are needed for geometrical isomers.

questions.q: A chiral carbon has…
questions.why: It gives non-superimposable mirror images (optical isomers).

questions.q: How many structural isomers have the molecular formula C₄H₉Br?
questions.why: 1-bromobutane, 2-bromobutane, 1-bromo-2-methylpropane and 2-bromo-2-methylpropane: two chain arrangements, each with two different positions for Br.

questions.q: The C–Br bond in bromoethane breaks heterolytically. Which pair of species forms?
questions.why: In heterolytic fission one atom keeps both bonding electrons; the more electronegative bromine takes them, giving a carbocation and a bromide ion. Homolytic fission gives the radicals.

long.q: Give the name and structural formula of a primary, a secondary and a tertiary alcohol with molecular formula C₄H₁₀O. State the type of isomerism shown between any of these alcohols and CH₃CH₂OCH₂CH₃.
scheme: B1: primary: butan-1-ol CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂OH (or 2-methylpropan-1-ol (CH₃)₂CHCH₂OH)
B1: secondary: butan-2-ol CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₃
B1: tertiary: 2-methylpropan-2-ol (CH₃)₃COH
B1: functional group isomerism (structural isomerism)

long.q: Explain why but-2-ene shows geometrical (cis/trans) isomerism but but-1-ene does not. Name the two geometrical isomers of but-2-ene.
scheme: B1: there is restricted rotation about the C=C bond (because of the π bond)
B1: in but-2-ene each carbon of the C=C has two different groups (H and CH₃)
B1: in but-1-ene one carbon of the C=C carries two identical groups (two H atoms)
B1: cis-but-2-ene and trans-but-2-ene (Z and E)

long.q: 2-hydroxypropanoic acid, CH₃CH(OH)COOH, shows optical isomerism. Identify its chiral centre, explain what is meant by a chiral centre, and state how the two optical isomers differ.
scheme: B1: the chiral centre is carbon 2, the C bonded to CH₃, OH, H and COOH
B1: a chiral centre is a carbon atom bonded to four different atoms or groups
B1: the two isomers are mirror images that cannot be superimposed
B1: they rotate plane-polarised light by equal amounts in opposite directions

long.q: Explain the terms homolytic fission, heterolytic fission, nucleophile and electrophile, giving an example of a species formed or acting in each case.
scheme: B1: homolytic fission: a covalent bond breaks with one electron going to each atom, forming free radicals, e.g. Cl₂ → 2Cl•
B1: heterolytic fission: one atom takes both bonding electrons, forming ions, e.g. a carbocation and Br⁻
B1: nucleophile: an electron-pair donor, e.g. OH⁻, CN⁻ or NH₃
B1: electrophile: an electron-pair acceptor, e.g. H⁺, NO₂⁺ or a carbocation

long.q: Classify each reaction by type: (i) ethene + bromine → 1,2-dibromoethane; (ii) bromoethane + aqueous NaOH → ethanol; (iii) ethanol passed over hot Al₂O₃ → ethene; (iv) ethanol + acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ → ethanal; (v) ethyl ethanoate + water (acid catalyst) → ethanoic acid + ethanol.
scheme: B1: (i) (electrophilic) addition
B1: (ii) (nucleophilic) substitution, also called hydrolysis
B1: (iii) elimination (dehydration)
B1: (iv) oxidation
B1: (v) hydrolysis

questions.q: Alkanes react with chlorine in UV light by…
questions.why: UV splits Cl₂ into radicals: initiation, propagation, termination.

questions.q: Ethene reacts with bromine by…
questions.why: The electron-rich C=C attacks the polarised Br₂.

questions.q: What is the mechanism when ethene reacts with hydrogen bromide?
questions.why: The electron-rich C=C attracts the δ+ hydrogen of HBr: an electrophile adds across the double bond.

questions.q: Which is a propagation step in the reaction of methane with chlorine in UV light?
questions.why: A propagation step uses one radical and produces another, so the chain continues; the first option is initiation and the two radical–radical combinations are termination.

questions.q: But-2-ene is heated with concentrated acidified potassium manganate(VII). What is the organic product?
questions.why: Hot concentrated KMnO₄ splits the C=C bond. Each CH₃CH= end becomes CH₃COOH, so CH₃CH=CHCH₃ gives two molecules of ethanoic acid. The diol forms with cold, dilute KMnO₄.

long.q: But-1-ene reacts with hydrogen bromide to give two products. Name the major product and explain why it is formed in the larger amount.
scheme: B1: 2-bromobutane
B1: via the secondary carbocation (CH₃CH⁺CH₂CH₃)
B1: which is more stable than the primary one, because alkyl groups push electrons towards (are electron-donating to) the positive carbon

long.q: Describe the mechanism of the reaction between methane and chlorine in ultraviolet light, naming each stage and giving equations. Explain why a mixture of chlorinated products is obtained.
scheme: B1: initiation: Cl₂ → 2Cl• (homolytic fission by UV light)
B1: propagation: Cl• + CH₄ → HCl + •CH₃
B1: propagation: •CH₃ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + Cl•
B1: termination: e.g. •CH₃ + •CH₃ → C₂H₆, or •CH₃ + Cl• → CH₃Cl, or 2Cl• → Cl₂
B1: Cl• can also attack CH₃Cl and further products, giving CH₂Cl₂, CHCl₃ and CCl₄ (further substitution)

long.q: Describe the mechanism of the reaction between ethene and bromine.
scheme: B1: as Br₂ approaches the π electrons of C=C, the Br–Br bond becomes polarised (Brδ+–Brδ−)
B1: the π electrons attack Brδ+ and the Br–Br bond breaks heterolytically, releasing Br⁻
B1: a carbocation intermediate, CH₂BrCH₂⁺, is formed
B1: Br⁻ uses a lone pair to bond to the positive carbon, giving 1,2-dibromoethane (electrophilic addition)

long.q: 2-methylbut-2-ene, (CH₃)₂C=CHCH₃, is reacted separately with cold dilute acidified potassium manganate(VII) and with hot concentrated acidified potassium manganate(VII). Give the colour change seen and name the organic product(s) in each case.
scheme: B1: in both cases the purple solution is decolourised
B1: cold dilute: 2-methylbutane-2,3-diol, (CH₃)₂C(OH)CH(OH)CH₃
B1: hot concentrated: the C=C is split; the (CH₃)₂C= end gives propanone
B1: the =CHCH₃ end gives ethanoic acid

long.q: Decane is cracked: C₁₀H₂₂ → C₈H₁₈ + X. Identify X, state the conditions used, and explain why cracking is economically important. Explain why carbon monoxide from the incomplete combustion of octane is harmful.
scheme: B1: X is ethene, C₂H₄
B1: high temperature with a catalyst such as Al₂O₃ (or zeolite)
B1: it converts long-chain fractions in low demand into shorter alkanes for fuel (petrol) and alkenes for making polymers
B1: CO is toxic: it binds to haemoglobin and reduces the blood's ability to carry oxygen

questions.q: Which halogenoalkane hydrolyses fastest?
questions.why: The C–I bond is the weakest, so it breaks most easily.

questions.q: Heating a halogenoalkane with ethanolic KOH mainly gives…
questions.why: In ethanol, OH⁻ acts as a base and removes HX.

questions.q: Which reagents and conditions convert a halogenoalkane into a nitrile?
o: KCN in ethanol, heat under reflux
questions.why: Examiners (2023): some gave the conditions for carbonyl → hydroxynitrile instead of halogenoalkane → nitrile.

questions.q: 2-bromo-2-methylpropane is hydrolysed by aqueous hydroxide ions by the SN1 mechanism. What is the first step?
o: OH⁻ attacks the carbon as the C–Br bond breaks, in one step
OH⁻ removes a hydrogen atom to form an alkene
The C–Br bond breaks heterolytically to form a tertiary carbocation and Br⁻
questions.why: In SN1 the slow first step is ionisation to a carbocation, which is stabilised by three alkyl groups; OH⁻ then attacks the carbocation. The one-step attack describes SN2.

questions.q: 1-chlorobutane is warmed with aqueous NaOH, then dilute nitric acid and aqueous silver nitrate are added. What is seen?
questions.why: Hydrolysis releases Cl⁻ ions, which give white AgCl. Nitric acid is added first to neutralise excess OH⁻, which would otherwise precipitate silver oxide.

long.q: Describe the SN2 mechanism for the reaction of bromoethane with hydroxide ions.
scheme: B1: the lone pair of OH⁻ attacks the δ+ carbon bonded to Br, from the side opposite the Br
B1: a transition state forms in which the C–OH bond is forming as the C–Br bond is breaking
B1: the C–Br bond breaks heterolytically and Br⁻ leaves, giving ethanol
B1: it happens in one step involving both bromoethane and OH⁻ (bimolecular)

long.q: 2-bromo-2-methylpropane reacts with aqueous hydroxide ions by an SN1 mechanism. Describe the two steps, and explain why this tertiary halogenoalkane reacts by SN1 rather than SN2.
scheme: B1: step 1 (slow): the C–Br bond breaks heterolytically to give the carbocation (CH₃)₃C⁺ and Br⁻
B1: step 2 (fast): OH⁻ bonds to the carbocation, giving 2-methylpropan-2-ol
B1: the tertiary carbocation is stabilised by three electron-donating (positive inductive) methyl groups
B1: the three bulky methyl groups hinder a nucleophile approaching the carbon (steric hindrance), so SN2 is difficult

long.q: 1-chlorobutane, 1-bromobutane and 1-iodobutane are warmed separately with silver nitrate in aqueous ethanol. Describe and explain the order in which precipitates appear.
scheme: B1: 1-iodobutane gives a yellow precipitate first, then 1-bromobutane (cream), then 1-chlorobutane (white) slowest
B1: the C–I bond is the weakest (lowest bond energy), C–Cl the strongest
B1: so C–I is hydrolysed fastest, releasing halide ions, which form AgX with Ag⁺
B1: bond strength matters more than bond polarity (C–Cl is the most polar but reacts slowest)

long.q: 2-bromopropane reacts with sodium hydroxide in two different ways depending on the conditions. For each, give the conditions, the organic product and the type of reaction.
scheme: B1: aqueous NaOH, warmed (under reflux): propan-2-ol
B1: nucleophilic substitution
B1: NaOH dissolved in ethanol, heated: propene
B1: elimination

long.q: Bromoethane is heated under reflux with potassium cyanide in ethanol. Name the organic product, state the type of reaction, and explain why this reaction is useful in synthesis. Give the conditions and organic product of the reaction of bromoethane with ammonia.
scheme: B1: propanenitrile, CH₃CH₂CN; nucleophilic substitution
B1: it adds one carbon atom, increasing the length of the carbon chain
B1: ammonia (in excess) in ethanol, heated under pressure (in a sealed tube)
B1: ethylamine, CH₃CH₂NH₂

questions.q: Which alcohol is NOT oxidised by acidified dichromate(VI)?
questions.why: Tertiary alcohols have no H on the carbon bearing the OH.

questions.q: Distilling a primary alcohol with acidified dichromate as it forms gives…
questions.why: Distilling removes the aldehyde before it oxidises further; heating under reflux gives the acid.

questions.q: Which alcohol is not oxidised by acidified potassium dichromate(VI)?
questions.why: Tertiary alcohols have no H on the C–OH carbon, so the orange dichromate stays orange.

questions.q: Which alcohol gives a yellow precipitate when warmed with alkaline aqueous iodine?
questions.why: The tri-iodomethane (CHI₃) test is positive for alcohols containing the CH₃CH(OH)– group; propan-2-ol, CH₃CH(OH)CH₃, has it, the others do not.

questions.q: Which reagent and conditions convert ethanol into ethene?
o: Pass the vapour over heated Al₂O₃
questions.why: Ethene forms by dehydration, which needs a heated Al₂O₃ catalyst (or hot concentrated H₂SO₄/H₃PO₄). Steam with H₃PO₄ is the reverse reaction, hydration of ethene.

long.q: Describe how you could use acidified potassium dichromate(VI) and one other reagent to distinguish between propan-1-ol, propan-2-ol and 2-methylpropan-2-ol.
scheme: B1: warm each with acidified K₂Cr₂O₇: propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol turn it orange to green
B1: 2-methylpropan-2-ol (tertiary) leaves it orange
B1: distil off the product: propan-1-ol gives an aldehyde, propan-2-ol a ketone
B1: Tollens' reagent gives a silver mirror with the aldehyde only (or Fehling's: red precipitate)

long.q: Ethanol reacts with sodium. Write the equation, describe what you would see, and explain why the reaction is less vigorous than that of sodium with water.
scheme: B1: 2C₂H₅OH + 2Na → 2C₂H₅ONa + H₂
B1: bubbles of gas form steadily and the sodium slowly disappears (it sinks, rather than racing around as on water)
B1: ethanol is a weaker acid than water (loses H⁺ less readily)
B1: the ethyl group is electron-donating, which increases the negative charge on the O of the ethoxide ion and makes it less stable than OH⁻

long.q: Give the equation and conditions for the industrial manufacture of ethanol from ethene. Then give the reagents, conditions and equation for converting ethanol into ethyl ethanoate.
scheme: B1: C₂H₄(g) + H₂O(g) ⇌ C₂H₅OH(g)
B1: steam, phosphoric(V) acid catalyst, about 300 °C and 6 MPa (60 atm)
B1: heat with ethanoic acid and a few drops of concentrated sulfuric acid as catalyst
B1: CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH ⇌ CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O

long.q: Describe the tri-iodomethane (iodoform) test. State which of methanol, ethanol, propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol give a positive result, and explain why.
scheme: B1: warm the compound with alkaline aqueous iodine (I₂ and NaOH)
B1: a positive result is a pale yellow precipitate of CHI₃ (with an antiseptic smell)
B1: ethanol and propan-2-ol give a positive result
B1: only they contain the CH₃CH(OH)– group (oxidised to CH₃CO–); methanol and propan-1-ol do not

long.q: Butan-2-ol is dehydrated by heating with concentrated phosphoric(V) acid. Name every alkene that can form, including stereoisomers. Give a reagent that converts butan-2-ol into 2-chlorobutane.
scheme: B1: elimination of H₂O can involve a hydrogen from either neighbouring carbon
B1: but-1-ene
B1: cis-but-2-ene and trans-but-2-ene (three alkenes in all)
B1: PCl₅ (or SOCl₂, or PCl₃ with heat)

questions.q: Which reagent distinguishes an aldehyde from a ketone?
questions.why: Aldehydes give a silver mirror; ketones don't. 2,4-DNPH reacts with both.

questions.q: NaBH₄ reduces a ketone to…
questions.why: Ketones are reduced to secondary alcohols.

questions.q: What is the product when propanone is reduced with NaBH₄?
questions.why: Ketones are reduced to secondary alcohols.

questions.q: Which reagent gives an orange precipitate with both aldehydes and ketones?
questions.why: 2,4-DNPH reacts with any C=O group in an aldehyde or ketone; the other three are oxidising agents that react only with aldehydes.

questions.q: Ethanal reacts with HCN in the presence of a little KCN. What are the mechanism and the product?
questions.why: CN⁻ attacks the δ+ carbonyl carbon and the intermediate is then protonated, giving CH₃CH(OH)CN: the OH and CN are on the same carbon, C-2 of the three-carbon chain.

long.q: Describe how you would prepare a sample of propanal from propan-1-ol, explaining how further oxidation is avoided, and how propanone could be prepared from propan-2-ol.
scheme: B1: warm propan-1-ol with acidified potassium dichromate(VI) (orange to green)
B1: distil off the propanal as soon as it forms (it has a lower boiling point than the alcohol)
B1: this removes it before it can be oxidised further to propanoic acid
B1: heat propan-2-ol under reflux with acidified dichromate(VI); the ketone propanone is not oxidised further

long.q: Ethanal reacts with hydrogen cyanide in the presence of a little potassium cyanide. Describe the mechanism and name the organic product.
scheme: B1: the nucleophile CN⁻ (from KCN) uses its lone pair to attack the δ+ carbon of C=O
B1: the π bond of C=O breaks and its electrons move onto oxygen, giving a negatively charged (alkoxide) intermediate
B1: the O⁻ takes H⁺ from HCN, regenerating CN⁻ (nucleophilic addition)
B1: product 2-hydroxypropanenitrile, CH₃CH(OH)CN

long.q: Describe how Fehling's solution and Tollens' reagent could each be used to distinguish propanal from propanone, and explain the chemistry of the positive results.
scheme: B1: warm with Fehling's solution: propanal gives a brick-red precipitate; propanone leaves it blue
B1: warm with Tollens' reagent: propanal gives a silver mirror (grey/black precipitate); propanone shows no change
B1: aldehydes are oxidised (to carboxylic acids / carboxylate ions); ketones are not
B1: Cu²⁺ is reduced to Cu⁺ (Cu₂O), and Ag⁺ is reduced to Ag

long.q: Butanone is reduced by sodium tetrahydridoborate(III), NaBH₄. Name the product, write an equation using [H], state the type of reaction, and explain whether the product is chiral.
scheme: B1: butan-2-ol
B1: CH₃COCH₂CH₃ + 2[H] → CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₃
B1: reduction (nucleophilic addition of hydride, H⁻)
B1: chiral: carbon 2 is bonded to four different groups (H, OH, CH₃ and C₂H₅)

long.q: Describe how 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine can be used to show that an unknown compound is a carbonyl compound and to identify it. Explain how alkaline aqueous iodine would distinguish butanone from pentan-3-one.
scheme: B1: add 2,4-DNPH: an orange (yellow-orange) precipitate shows a C=O group in an aldehyde or ketone
B1: filter and recrystallise the precipitate, then measure its melting point
B1: compare the melting point with known values for 2,4-DNPH derivatives to identify the carbonyl compound
B1: warm with alkaline iodine: butanone gives a pale yellow precipitate of CHI₃; pentan-3-one gives none
B1: butanone contains the CH₃CO– group; pentan-3-one (CH₃CH₂COCH₂CH₃) does not

questions.q: An alcohol and a carboxylic acid with a concentrated H₂SO₄ catalyst form…
questions.why: Esterification (a condensation reaction).

questions.q: Carboxylic acids react with sodium carbonate to give…
questions.why: They are acidic enough to release CO₂ from carbonates.

questions.q: Ethanoic acid is warmed with ethanol and a little concentrated sulfuric acid. What forms?
questions.why: This is esterification; the acid is a catalyst and the reaction is reversible.

questions.q: Which reagent reduces ethanoic acid to ethanol?
o: H₂ with a nickel catalyst at room temperature
questions.why: Carboxylic acids need the powerful reducing agent LiAlH₄; NaBH₄ reduces aldehydes and ketones but not carboxylic acids, and dichromate is an oxidising agent.

questions.q: Ethyl propanoate is heated under reflux with aqueous sodium hydroxide. What are the products?
questions.why: Alkaline hydrolysis of CH₃CH₂COOCH₂CH₃ gives the alcohol and the carboxylate salt (not the free acid). The acid part of the ester is propanoate; the alcohol part is ethanol.

long.q: Describe two ways of making propanoic acid, one from an alcohol and one from a nitrile, giving the reagents, conditions and an equation for each.
scheme: B1: heat propan-1-ol under reflux with excess acidified potassium dichromate(VI)
B1: CH₃CH₂CH₂OH + 2[O] → CH₃CH₂COOH + H₂O
B1: heat propanenitrile under reflux with dilute hydrochloric (or sulfuric) acid
B1: CH₃CH₂CN + 2H₂O + HCl → CH₃CH₂COOH + NH₄Cl

long.q: Write equations for the reactions of ethanoic acid with magnesium, with aqueous sodium hydroxide and with sodium carbonate. Describe what you would see in the reaction with sodium carbonate and how you would identify the gas.
scheme: B1: 2CH₃COOH + Mg → (CH₃COO)₂Mg + H₂
B1: CH₃COOH + NaOH → CH₃COONa + H₂O
B1: 2CH₃COOH + Na₂CO₃ → 2CH₃COONa + H₂O + CO₂
B1: effervescence; the gas turns limewater milky (cloudy)

long.q: Methyl propanoate is hydrolysed by heating under reflux with (i) dilute sulfuric acid and (ii) aqueous sodium hydroxide. Name the products of each, and explain why the alkaline hydrolysis goes to completion but the acid hydrolysis does not.
scheme: B1: (i) propanoic acid and methanol
B1: acid hydrolysis is reversible and reaches an equilibrium
B1: (ii) sodium propanoate and methanol
B1: the carboxylate ion does not react with methanol, so the reverse reaction cannot happen

long.q: 6.00 g of ethanoic acid is heated with excess ethanol and a little concentrated sulfuric acid, giving 5.28 g of ethyl ethanoate. Calculate the percentage yield, and suggest one reason it is less than 100%. (Mr: CH₃COOH 60.0, CH₃COOC₂H₅ 88.0)
scheme: M1: n(ethanoic acid) = 6.00 ÷ 60.0 = 0.100 mol
M1: maximum mass of ester = 0.100 × 88.0 = 8.80 g
B1: esterification is reversible, so it reaches equilibrium (or product is lost during separation and purification)

long.q: Butanoic acid is reduced by lithium tetrahydridoaluminate(III), LiAlH₄. Name the product, write an equation using [H], explain why dry ether is used as the solvent, and give a simple test to distinguish butanoic acid from the product.
scheme: B1: butan-1-ol
B1: CH₃CH₂CH₂COOH + 4[H] → CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂OH + H₂O
B1: LiAlH₄ reacts violently with water, so it must be kept dry
B1: add sodium carbonate (or hydrogencarbonate): butanoic acid fizzes (CO₂), butan-1-ol does not

questions.q: A nitrile is hydrolysed by heating with dilute acid. It forms…
questions.why: R–C≡N + 2H₂O + H⁺ → RCOOH + NH₄⁺.

questions.q: Reacting a halogenoalkane with KCN in ethanol…
o: lengthens the carbon chain by one
questions.why: CN⁻ substitutes for the halogen, adding a carbon.

questions.q: How is a primary amine made from a halogenoalkane?
o: Heat with excess ethanolic ammonia in a sealed tube
React with hydrogen and a nickel catalyst
questions.why: Excess ammonia reduces further substitution to secondary and tertiary amines.

questions.q: Which reagent converts propanenitrile, CH₃CH₂CN, into propylamine, CH₃CH₂CH₂NH₂?
questions.why: The C≡N group is reduced to –CH₂NH₂ by H₂/Ni (or LiAlH₄). Heating with dilute acid hydrolyses the nitrile to a carboxylic acid instead.

questions.q: Why is excess ammonia used when making ethylamine from bromoethane?
o: To stop the bromoethane being hydrolysed to ethanol
To make it less likely that the ethylamine formed reacts further with bromoethane
questions.why: Ethylamine is itself a nucleophile and can attack more bromoethane to give secondary and tertiary amines; a large excess of NH₃ makes ammonia the most likely nucleophile.

long.q: Bromoethane is heated with ammonia in ethanol in a sealed tube. Write an equation for the formation of ethylamine, and explain why diethylamine is also formed and how the proportion of ethylamine can be increased.
scheme: B1: CH₃CH₂Br + 2NH₃ → CH₃CH₂NH₂ + NH₄Br
B1: ethylamine has a lone pair on nitrogen, so it is also a nucleophile
B1: it reacts with more bromoethane to give diethylamine, (CH₃CH₂)₂NH
B1: use a large excess of ammonia

long.q: 2-hydroxypropanoic acid can be made from ethanal in two steps. Give the reagents and conditions for each step and the intermediate formed. When 2.20 g of ethanal is used, 2.70 g of 2-hydroxypropanoic acid is obtained; calculate the overall percentage yield. (Mr: ethanal 44.0, 2-hydroxypropanoic acid 90.0)
scheme: B1: step 1: HCN with a little KCN (catalyst / source of CN⁻), at about 10–20 °C
B1: intermediate: 2-hydroxypropanenitrile, CH₃CH(OH)CN
B1: step 2: heat under reflux with dilute acid (HCl or H₂SO₄)
B1: the nitrile group is hydrolysed to –COOH
M1: n(ethanal) = 2.20 ÷ 44.0 = 0.0500 mol, so maximum mass = 0.0500 × 90.0 = 4.50 g

long.q: Ethanenitrile is hydrolysed by heating under reflux (i) with dilute hydrochloric acid and (ii) with aqueous sodium hydroxide. Write an equation for each. How could you show that a gas is released in (ii), and how would you obtain ethanoic acid from the mixture in (ii)?
scheme: B1: CH₃CN + 2H₂O + HCl → CH₃COOH + NH₄Cl
B1: CH₃CN + NaOH + H₂O → CH₃COONa + NH₃
B1: ammonia turns damp red litmus paper blue
B1: acidify with a strong acid (e.g. dilute HCl) to convert ethanoate ions into ethanoic acid

long.q: Propanone reacts with HCN in the presence of KCN. Give the structural formula and name of the product. Explain why KCN is needed, and why the reaction must be done in a fume cupboard.
scheme: B1: (CH₃)₂C(OH)CN, 2-hydroxy-2-methylpropanenitrile
B1: HCN is a very weak acid, so it gives very few CN⁻ ions
B1: KCN supplies CN⁻, the nucleophile that attacks the carbonyl carbon
B1: HCN is highly toxic and volatile (so it is often generated in the mixture from KCN and acid)

long.q: Give the structural formulae and names of the two amines with molecular formula C₂H₇N. Classify each as primary or secondary, explaining the difference, and suggest reagents to make the secondary amine from a halogenoalkane.
scheme: B1: ethylamine, CH₃CH₂NH₂: primary
B1: dimethylamine, (CH₃)₂NH: secondary
B1: a primary amine has one alkyl group on the nitrogen; a secondary amine has two
B1: bromomethane (or chloromethane) heated with methylamine in ethanol (CH₃NH₂ + CH₃Br → (CH₃)₂NH + HBr)

questions.q: What is the repeat unit of poly(propene)?
questions.why: Opening propene's C=C gives –CH₂–CH(CH₃)–.

questions.q: Why are poly(alkenes) hard to dispose of?
questions.why: Strong, non-polar C–C and C–H bonds; burning them can release toxic gases.

questions.q: Why are addition polymers like poly(ethene) hard to dispose of?
o: They are non-biodegradable because of strong non-polar C–C and C–H bonds
questions.why: Burning them can release toxic gases.

questions.q: Which monomer forms the addition polymer with repeat unit –CH₂–CHCl–?
questions.why: Addition polymers form from alkenes; CH₂=CHCl (chloroethene) opens its C=C bond to give –CH₂–CHCl– (PVC). Chloroethane has no C=C bond.

questions.q: Why can burning waste poly(chloroethene) (PVC) be hazardous?
o: It produces toxic, acidic hydrogen chloride gas
It produces only carbon dioxide and water
It explodes because it contains oxygen
questions.why: The chlorine in the polymer ends up as HCl (and other toxic chlorinated compounds) when PVC is burned.

long.q: Give the repeat units of poly(propene) and poly(chloroethene), and explain why the formation of these polymers is called addition polymerisation.
scheme: B1: poly(propene): –CH₂–CH(CH₃)–
B1: poly(chloroethene): –CH₂–CHCl–
B1: the π bond of the C=C in each monomer opens and the monomers join, with no other product formed

long.q: Perspex has the repeat unit –CH₂–C(CH₃)(COOCH₃)–. Give the structural formula of its monomer, and name the two functional groups in the monomer.
scheme: B1: CH₂=C(CH₃)COOCH₃ (methyl 2-methylpropenoate)
B1: alkene (C=C)
B1: ester

long.q: Explain why poly(alkenes) are difficult to dispose of, and describe the problems caused by disposing of them in landfill and by burning, with particular reference to PVC.
scheme: B1: they are non-biodegradable: chemically inert because of strong, non-polar C–C and C–H bonds
B1: in landfill they persist for many years and take up space
B1: burning releases CO₂ (a greenhouse gas) and possibly toxic CO
B1: burning PVC also releases toxic, acidic HCl (and other toxic chlorinated compounds)

long.q: A sample of poly(ethene) has an average relative molecular mass of 2.8 × 10⁵. Calculate the average number of ethene units per chain, and explain why poly(ethene) softens over a range of temperatures rather than melting sharply.
scheme: M1: Mr of ethene, C₂H₄ = 28.0
A1: number of units = 2.8 × 10⁵ ÷ 28.0 = 1.0 × 10⁴
B1: the chains have different lengths (termination is random), so the strength of the intermolecular forces varies from chain to chain

long.q: Phenylethene, C₆H₅CH=CH₂, is polymerised. Name the polymer and give its repeat unit. Explain why the monomer decolourises bromine water but the polymer does not.
scheme: B1: poly(phenylethene) (polystyrene)
B1: –CH₂–CH(C₆H₅)–
B1: the monomer has a C=C bond, which undergoes electrophilic addition with bromine (orange to colourless)
B1: the polymer's chain is saturated (the C=C has been used up), so the bromine water stays orange

questions.q: To go from ethanol to ethanoic acid, use…
questions.why: Full oxidation of a primary alcohol under reflux.

questions.q: Which reaction adds one carbon atom to a carbon chain?
questions.why: The nitrile formed can then be hydrolysed or reduced.

questions.q: Which conditions convert a nitrile into a carboxylic acid?
o: Heat under reflux with dilute acid
questions.why: Acid hydrolysis turns –C≡N into –COOH; reduction would give an amine.

questions.q: Which two-step route converts propene into propanone?
o: Step 1: steam with H₃PO₄ catalyst; step 2: heat with acidified K₂Cr₂O₇
Step 1: H₂ with Ni; step 2: acidified K₂Cr₂O₇
Step 1: steam with H₃PO₄ catalyst; step 2: NaBH₄
questions.why: Hydration of propene gives mainly propan-2-ol (via the more stable secondary carbocation), and oxidising a secondary alcohol gives the ketone. NaBH₄ is a reducing agent.

questions.q: Compound X decolourises bromine water and gives effervescence with aqueous sodium carbonate. Which could X be?
questions.why: Decolourising bromine water shows a C=C bond, and effervescence (CO₂) with Na₂CO₃ shows a carboxylic acid; only propenoic acid has both.

long.q: Suggest a two-step synthesis of propanone from propene. For each step give the reagents and conditions, the product and the type of reaction.
scheme: B1: step 1: steam with a phosphoric(V) acid catalyst at high temperature and pressure
B1: gives propan-2-ol (the major product); electrophilic addition (hydration)
B1: step 2: heat under reflux with acidified potassium dichromate(VI)
B1: oxidation of the secondary alcohol to propanone

long.q: Compound Q is HOCH₂CH=CHCHO. Name the three functional groups in Q, and predict what you would see when Q is treated with: bromine water; Tollens' reagent (warmed); sodium metal; 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine.
scheme: B1: primary alcohol, alkene and aldehyde
B1: bromine water is decolourised (orange to colourless), by the C=C
B1: a silver mirror forms, by the aldehyde
B1: fizzing (hydrogen), by the –OH group
B1: an orange precipitate forms, by the C=O

long.q: Propane-1,2-diol can be made from propan-1-ol in three steps, via propene and 1,2-dibromopropane. Give the reagents and conditions for each step and name the type of each reaction.
scheme: B1: step 1: pass propan-1-ol vapour over heated Al₂O₃ (or heat with concentrated H₃PO₄)
B1: elimination (dehydration) giving propene
B1: step 2: bromine at room temperature: electrophilic addition giving 1,2-dibromopropane
B1: step 3: heat under reflux with aqueous sodium hydroxide
B1: nucleophilic substitution (hydrolysis) giving propane-1,2-diol

long.q: Suggest a three-step synthesis of propanoic acid from ethanol. Give the reagents and conditions for each step and the intermediates, and identify the step that increases the length of the carbon chain.
scheme: B1: step 1: NaBr with concentrated H₂SO₄ (or PBr₃), heat: bromoethane
B1: step 2: KCN in ethanol, heat under reflux
B1: intermediate propanenitrile, CH₃CH₂CN
B1: step 3: heat under reflux with dilute acid (HCl), hydrolysing the nitrile to propanoic acid
B1: step 2 lengthens the chain: nucleophilic substitution by CN⁻ adds a carbon

long.q: Explain why some organic preparations are heated under reflux, while in others the product is distilled off as it forms. Give an example of each.
scheme: B1: under reflux, vapours condense and drip back into the flask, so volatile reactants and products are not lost
B1: so the mixture can be heated for a long time to complete a slow reaction, e.g. oxidising a primary alcohol fully to a carboxylic acid
B1: distillation removes a volatile product from the mixture as soon as it forms (separation by boiling point)
B1: e.g. distilling off an aldehyde as it forms so it is not oxidised further to a carboxylic acid

questions.q: A broad IR absorption at 2500–3000 cm⁻¹ with a peak near 1700 cm⁻¹ suggests…
questions.why: Broad O–H (acid) plus C=O.

questions.q: In a mass spectrum, the M⁺ peak gives the…
questions.why: The molecular ion peak is at the Mr (the M+1 peak hints at the carbon count).

questions.q: What causes the small M+1 peak in a mass spectrum?
questions.why: About 1.1% of carbon is ¹³C, so the M+1 height helps count the carbon atoms.

questions.q: A compound shows a strong infrared absorption near 1715 cm⁻¹, sharp C–H absorptions near 2900 cm⁻¹, and no broad absorption anywhere between 2500 and 3600 cm⁻¹. Which compound could it be?
questions.why: The 1715 cm⁻¹ peak is C=O; the absence of any broad O–H absorption rules out alcohols and carboxylic acids.

questions.q: The mass spectrum of a bromoalkane shows molecular ion peaks at m/e 122 and 124. What are their approximate relative heights?
questions.why: Bromine has two isotopes, ⁷⁹Br and ⁸¹Br, in roughly equal amounts, so a molecule with one Br gives M and M+2 peaks of about equal height. 3 : 1 is the pattern for one chlorine atom.

long.q: Compound X, C₃H₆O₂, has an infrared spectrum with a very broad absorption between 2500 and 3000 cm⁻¹ and a strong absorption at 1710 cm⁻¹. Identify the bonds responsible and deduce the structure of X. Explain how the spectrum rules out the isomer methyl ethanoate.
scheme: B1: the broad band at 2500–3000 cm⁻¹ is O–H in a carboxylic acid (hydrogen bonded)
B1: the strong band at 1710 cm⁻¹ is C=O
B1: X is propanoic acid, CH₃CH₂COOH
B1: methyl ethanoate (an ester) would show C=O but no broad O–H absorption

long.q: In the mass spectrum of a hydrocarbon, the molecular ion peak at m/z = 86 has a relative abundance of 40.0 and the M+1 peak has a relative abundance of 2.64. Calculate the number of carbon atoms in a molecule and deduce the molecular formula.
scheme: M1: n = (100 × abundance of M+1) ÷ (1.1 × abundance of M⁺)
A1: C₆H₁₄ (86 − 72 = 14 hydrogen atoms)

long.q: The mass spectrum of a halogenoalkane has two molecular ion peaks, at m/z = 108 and 110, of almost equal height. Explain this, identify the compound, and state how the pattern would differ for a compound with one chlorine atom.
scheme: B1: two molecular ion peaks two mass units apart show one bromine atom
B1: bromine has two isotopes, ⁷⁹Br and ⁸¹Br, of roughly equal abundance (1 : 1)
B1: 108 − 79 = 29, which is C₂H₅, so the compound is bromoethane, C₂H₅Br
B1: one Cl atom gives M and M+2 peaks in the ratio 3 : 1 (³⁵Cl and ³⁷Cl)

long.q: A ketone with molecular formula C₅H₁₀O has a mass spectrum with large peaks at m/z = 57 and 29, but no peaks at m/z = 43 or 71. Identify the fragments responsible and deduce which ketone it is, explaining why it is not pentan-2-one.
scheme: B1: m/z 57 is CH₃CH₂CO⁺
B1: m/z 29 is CH₃CH₂⁺
B1: the ketone is pentan-3-one, CH₃CH₂COCH₂CH₃
B1: pentan-2-one, CH₃COCH₂CH₂CH₃, would give peaks at 43 (CH₃CO⁺) and 71 (C₃H₇CO⁺)

long.q: A compound contains only C, H and O and its molecular ion is at m/z = 60. Its infrared spectrum has a broad absorption at 3200–3600 cm⁻¹ and no absorption between 1670 and 1740 cm⁻¹. Its mass spectrum has a large peak at m/z = 31. Identify the compound, explaining each piece of evidence.
scheme: B1: broad 3200–3600 cm⁻¹ is O–H of an alcohol; no C=O (so not ethanoic acid, also Mr 60)
B1: an alcohol of Mr 60 is C₃H₈O: propan-1-ol or propan-2-ol
B1: m/z 31 is CH₂OH⁺
B1: CH₂OH⁺ forms from propan-1-ol, CH₃CH₂CH₂OH (propan-2-ol would give CH₃CHOH⁺ at 45)

questions.q: A reaction is feasible when ΔG is…
questions.why: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS ≤ 0 for a feasible reaction.

questions.q: Lattice energy becomes more exothermic when ions are…
questions.why: Smaller, more highly charged ions attract more strongly.

questions.q: Which change has a positive entropy change?
o: A solid dissolving to make aqueous ions
questions.why: Particles become more disordered (more ways to arrange energy).

questions.q: For CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g), ΔH = +178 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS = +161 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Above what temperature is the reaction feasible?
questions.why: Feasible when ΔG = ΔH − TΔS ≤ 0, so T ≥ ΔH/ΔS = 178 000 J mol⁻¹ ÷ 161 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ = 1106 K. Not converting kJ to J gives 1.11 K.

questions.q: The lattice energy of NaCl is −787 kJ mol⁻¹. The enthalpy changes of hydration are Na⁺ −406 kJ mol⁻¹ and Cl⁻ −378 kJ mol⁻¹. What is the enthalpy change of solution of NaCl?
questions.why: ΔHsol = −(lattice energy) + ΣΔHhyd = +787 + (−406 − 378) = +3 kJ mol⁻¹: breaking the lattice needs slightly more energy than hydration releases.

long.q: Use the following data (kJ mol⁻¹) to calculate the lattice energy of sodium chloride: ΔHf NaCl −411; atomisation Na +107; first IE Na +496; atomisation Cl +122; first electron affinity Cl −349.
scheme: M1: a correct Born–Haber cycle

long.q: Define lattice energy. Explain why the lattice energy of magnesium oxide is much more exothermic than that of sodium chloride, and why that of sodium fluoride is more exothermic than that of sodium chloride.
scheme: B1: the enthalpy change when one mole of an ionic compound is formed from its gaseous ions (under standard conditions)
B1: Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ carry double the charges of Na⁺ and Cl⁻, so the electrostatic attraction is much stronger
B1: Mg²⁺ is also smaller than Na⁺ (and O²⁻ smaller than Cl⁻), so the ions are closer together
B1: F⁻ is smaller than Cl⁻, so in NaF the ions are closer and attract more strongly

long.q: The lattice energy of magnesium chloride is −2526 kJ mol⁻¹. The enthalpy changes of hydration are Mg²⁺ −1920 kJ mol⁻¹ and Cl⁻ −364 kJ mol⁻¹. Calculate the enthalpy change of solution of magnesium chloride, and explain why the hydration enthalpy of Mg²⁺ is much more exothermic than that of Cl⁻.
scheme: M1: ΔHsol = ΣΔHhyd − ΔHlatt (a correct energy cycle)
B1: Mg²⁺ is small with a 2+ charge (high charge density), so it attracts the δ− oxygen of water molecules much more strongly

long.q: For CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g), ΔH° = +178 kJ mol⁻¹. Standard entropies (J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹): CaCO₃ 92.9, CaO 39.7, CO₂ 213.6. Calculate ΔS°, show whether the reaction is feasible at 298 K, and calculate the minimum temperature at which it becomes feasible.
scheme: M1: ΔS° = ΣS(products) − ΣS(reactants) = (39.7 + 213.6) − 92.9
A1: ΔS° = +160.4 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹
M1: ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS° with ΔS° in kJ: 178 − 298 × 0.1604
A1: ΔG° = +130 kJ mol⁻¹, positive, so not feasible at 298 K
M1: feasible when ΔG° ≤ 0, so T = ΔH° ÷ ΔS° = 178 ÷ 0.1604
long.ans: +160 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹; +130 kJ mol⁻¹; 1110 K

long.q: Predict, with a reason, the sign of the entropy change for: (i) H₂O(l) → H₂O(g); (ii) N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g); (iii) 2Mg(s) + O₂(g) → 2MgO(s). Explain why an exothermic reaction with a negative entropy change can stop being feasible at high temperature.
scheme: B1: (i) positive: a gas is much more disordered (more ways of arranging particles and energy) than a liquid
B1: (ii) negative: 4 moles of gas become 2 moles of gas
B1: (iii) negative: a gas is used up and only a solid forms
B1: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS; with ΔS negative the −TΔS term is positive and grows with T, until it outweighs the negative ΔH and ΔG becomes positive

questions.q: Cu²⁺/Cu E° = +0.34 V and Zn²⁺/Zn E° = −0.76 V. What is the cell e.m.f.?
questions.why: E°cell = E°(positive) − E°(negative) = 0.34 − (−0.76) = 1.10 V.

questions.q: How much charge passes when 0.20 A flows for 965 s? (F = 96 500 C mol⁻¹)
o: Both: 193 C, which is 0.0020 mol of electrons
questions.why: Q = It = 193 C; 193 ÷ 96 500 = 0.0020 mol of electrons.

questions.q: Standard electrode potentials are measured against which reference?
questions.why: Standard conditions: 298 K, 100 kPa, 1.00 mol dm⁻³ solutions; the hydrogen electrode is defined as 0.00 V.

questions.q: What is true when a chemical electrochemical cell reaches equilibrium?
o: The standard electrode potential E° becomes 0 V
