The cell potential E_cell becomes 0 V
questions.why: At equilibrium, the driving force (Gibbs free energy change ΔG) is zero, so the operating cell voltage drops to zero.

questions.q: For Cu²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ ⇌ Cu(s), E° = +0.34 V. What is the electrode potential at 298 K when [Cu²⁺] = 0.010 mol dm⁻³? (E = E° + (0.059/z) log[oxidised form])
questions.why: E = 0.34 + (0.059 ÷ 2) × log 0.010 = 0.34 + 0.0295 × (−2) = +0.28 V. Lowering [Cu²⁺] makes the potential less positive; forgetting z = 2 gives +0.22 V.

long.q: Use E° values (Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺ +0.77 V; Cu²⁺/Cu +0.34 V) to calculate E°cell and predict whether Fe³⁺ ions oxidise copper.
scheme: B1: positive, so the reaction 2Fe³⁺ + Cu → 2Fe²⁺ + Cu²⁺ is feasible

long.q: Describe the standard hydrogen electrode, and explain how it would be used to measure the standard electrode potential of the Zn²⁺/Zn half-cell.
scheme: B1: a platinum (platinised) electrode dipping into 1.00 mol dm⁻³ H⁺(aq), e.g. HCl
B1: hydrogen gas at 100 kPa (1 atm) bubbled over the platinum, at 298 K
B1: connected to a zinc rod in 1.00 mol dm⁻³ Zn²⁺(aq) at 298 K
B1: the solutions are joined by a salt bridge (e.g. filter paper soaked in KNO₃) and the electrodes by a high-resistance voltmeter
B1: the voltmeter reads −0.76 V; zinc is the negative electrode

long.q: Aqueous copper(II) sulfate is electrolysed using copper electrodes with a current of 0.500 A for 40.0 minutes. Calculate the mass of copper deposited on the cathode. (F = 96 500 C mol⁻¹; Ar Cu = 63.5)

E° for Fe³⁺ + e⁻ ⇌ Fe²⁺ is +0.77 V. Use the Nernst equation to calculate the electrode potential when [Fe³⁺] = 0.100 mol dm⁻³ and [Fe²⁺] = 0.0100 mol dm⁻³, and state how the potential changes if [Fe²⁺] is increased.
scheme: M1: E = E° + (0.059 ÷ z) log([oxidised] ÷ [reduced])
B1: increasing [Fe²⁺] makes E less positive (the equilibrium shifts left, so the half-cell is a weaker oxidising agent)

long.q: Predict the product at each electrode when (i) concentrated aqueous sodium chloride and (ii) dilute aqueous sodium sulfate are electrolysed with inert electrodes. Explain your predictions and give the half-equations for the products formed in (ii).
scheme: B1: hydrogen forms at the cathode in both, because E° for Na⁺/Na (−2.71 V) is far more negative than for water / H⁺, so water is reduced instead
B1: (i) chlorine forms at the anode because Cl⁻ is present at high concentration
B1: (ii) oxygen forms at the anode because sulfate ions are not oxidised
B1: cathode 2H₂O + 2e⁻ → H₂ + 2OH⁻; anode 2H₂O → O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ (or 4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻)

questions.q: What is the pH of 0.010 mol dm⁻³ HCl?
A buffer resists pH change because…
o: it contains a weak acid and its conjugate base that remove added H⁺ or OH⁻
questions.why: Large reservoirs of HA and A⁻ absorb small additions.

questions.q: Ka for a weak acid is 1.0 × 10⁻⁵. What is its pKa?
questions.why: pKa = −log Ka = 5.

questions.q: What is the pH of an equimolar buffer solution containing ethanoic acid (pKa = 4.76) and sodium ethanoate?
questions.why: By the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation, pH = pKa + log([salt]/[acid]). When [salt] = [acid], log(1) = 0 so pH = pKa.

questions.q: For N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g), the equilibrium mixture at a total pressure of 200 kPa has a mole fraction of NO₂ of 0.40. What is Kp?
questions.why: p(NO₂) = 0.40 × 200 = 80 kPa and p(N₂O₄) = 0.60 × 200 = 120 kPa, so Kp = p(NO₂)² ÷ p(N₂O₄) = 6400 ÷ 120 = 53.3 kPa.

long.q: Calculate the pH of 0.10 mol dm⁻³ ethanoic acid (Ka = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³).

A buffer solution contains 0.200 mol dm⁻³ ethanoic acid and 0.100 mol dm⁻³ sodium ethanoate (Ka = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³). Calculate its pH, and explain how it keeps its pH almost constant when a small amount of acid is added.
scheme: M1: [H⁺] = Ka × [CH₃COOH] ÷ [CH₃COO⁻]
B1: added H⁺ ions react with the ethanoate ions: CH₃COO⁻ + H⁺ → CH₃COOH
B1: there are large amounts of both CH₃COOH and CH₃COO⁻, so their ratio, and so [H⁺], hardly changes

long.q: 1.00 mol of dinitrogen tetroxide is allowed to reach equilibrium: N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g). At equilibrium 20.0% of the N₂O₄ has dissociated and the total pressure is 150 kPa. Calculate Kp, giving its units.
scheme: M1: at equilibrium n(N₂O₄) = 0.800 mol and n(NO₂) = 0.400 mol
M1: total = 1.20 mol; mole fractions N₂O₄ 0.667, NO₂ 0.333
A1: partial pressures: N₂O₄ 100 kPa, NO₂ 50.0 kPa
M1: Kp = p(NO₂)² ÷ p(N₂O₄)

long.q: The solubility product of calcium fluoride is 3.2 × 10⁻¹¹ mol³ dm⁻⁹. Write the expression for Ksp, calculate the solubility of calcium fluoride in mol dm⁻³, and explain why it is less soluble in aqueous sodium fluoride than in water.
scheme: B1: Ksp = [Ca²⁺][F⁻]²
M1: if solubility = s, Ksp = s × (2s)² = 4s³
B1: the extra F⁻ (common ion) shifts CaF₂ ⇌ Ca²⁺ + 2F⁻ to the left, so less CaF₂ dissolves before [Ca²⁺][F⁻]² reaches Ksp

long.q: Calculate the pH of 0.0500 mol dm⁻³ barium hydroxide at 298 K (Kw = 1.00 × 10⁻¹⁴ mol² dm⁻⁶). At 50 °C, Kw = 5.5 × 10⁻¹⁴ mol² dm⁻⁶: calculate the pH of pure water at this temperature and explain why it is still neutral.
scheme: M1: Ba(OH)₂ is fully dissociated, so [OH⁻] = 2 × 0.0500 = 0.100 mol dm⁻³
M1: [H⁺] = Kw ÷ [OH⁻] = 1.00 × 10⁻¹³ mol dm⁻³
B1: it is neutral because [H⁺] still equals [OH⁻]

questions.q: Doubling [A] quadruples the rate. The order with respect to A is…
questions.why: rate ∝ [A]ⁿ and 2ⁿ = 4, so n = 2.

questions.q: The half-life of a first-order reaction…
questions.why: First-order half-lives are independent of concentration.

questions.q: Rate = k[A]²[B], with concentrations in mol dm⁻³ and time in s. What are the units of k?
questions.why: Overall order 3: k = rate ÷ (mol dm⁻³)³.

questions.q: A first-order reaction has a half-life of 20 s. What fraction of the reactant remains after 60 s?
questions.why: 60 s is three half-lives, and each one halves the amount: ½ × ½ × ½ = 1/8.

questions.q: The hydrolysis of 2-bromo-2-methylpropane by OH⁻ has the rate equation rate = k[(CH₃)₃CBr]. What does this suggest about the mechanism?
o: OH⁻ is not involved in the reaction at all
The reaction happens in a single step involving both reactants
The rate-determining step involves only (CH₃)₃CBr, and OH⁻ reacts in a later, faster step
questions.why: Only species in or before the rate-determining step appear in the rate equation. Zero order in OH⁻ means it reacts after the slow step (ionisation to a carbocation), consistent with SN1.

long.q: For the reaction A + B → C, doubling [A] doubles the rate and doubling [B] quadruples the rate. Write the rate equation and give the units of k when concentrations are in mol dm⁻³ and the rate in mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹.
scheme: B1: first order in A, second order in B
B1: rate = k[A][B]²
A1: units dm⁶ mol⁻² s⁻¹

long.q: The decomposition of a compound is first order with a half-life of 20.0 minutes. Calculate the rate constant in s⁻¹, find the time taken for the concentration to fall to 12.5% of its initial value, and state how the half-life would show that the reaction is first order.
scheme: M1: k = 0.693 ÷ t½ with t½ = 1200 s
B1: 12.5% is three half-lives: 60.0 minutes
B1: the half-life is constant, whatever the starting concentration

long.q: For the reaction NO₂(g) + CO(g) → NO(g) + CO₂(g) at low temperature, the rate equation is rate = k[NO₂]². Suggest a two-step mechanism consistent with this, identify the rate-determining step, and explain why [CO] does not appear in the rate equation.
scheme: B1: step 1 (slow): NO₂ + NO₂ → NO₃ + NO
B1: step 2 (fast): NO₃ + CO → NO₂ + CO₂
B1: the slow, rate-determining step involves two NO₂ molecules, so the rate depends on [NO₂]²
B1: CO only takes part in a fast step after the rate-determining step, so the reaction is zero order in CO

long.q: Initial rates for A + B → products at constant temperature: Experiment 1: [A] = 0.10, [B] = 0.10 mol dm⁻³, rate 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹. Experiment 2: [A] = 0.20, [B] = 0.10, rate 8.0 × 10⁻⁴. Experiment 3: [A] = 0.10, [B] = 0.30, rate 2.0 × 10⁻⁴. Deduce the order with respect to each reactant, write the rate equation and calculate k with its units.
scheme: B1: second order in A: doubling [A] (experiments 1 and 2) quadruples the rate
B1: zero order in B: tripling [B] (experiments 1 and 3) does not change the rate
B1: rate = k[A]²
A1: k = 2.0 × 10⁻² dm³ mol⁻¹ s⁻¹
long.ans: rate = k[A]²; k = 2.0 × 10⁻² dm³ mol⁻¹ s⁻¹

long.q: The reaction between peroxodisulfate ions and iodide ions, S₂O₈²⁻ + 2I⁻ → 2SO₄²⁻ + I₂, is slow but is catalysed by Fe²⁺ ions. Explain why the uncatalysed reaction is slow, and how Fe²⁺ ions act as a catalyst, with equations.
scheme: B1: both reactants are negative ions, which repel each other, so the activation energy is high
B1: S₂O₈²⁻ + 2Fe²⁺ → 2SO₄²⁻ + 2Fe³⁺
B1: 2Fe³⁺ + 2I⁻ → 2Fe²⁺ + I₂
B1: each step is between oppositely charged ions (lower Ea), and Fe²⁺ is regenerated; it is a homogeneous catalyst because it is in the same phase

questions.q: Down Group 2, the solubility of the sulfates…
questions.why: Hydration enthalpy falls faster than lattice energy as the cation gets bigger.

questions.q: How does the thermal stability of the Group 2 carbonates change down the group?
questions.why: Higher temperatures are needed to decompose carbonates further down the group.

questions.q: Why do Group 2 carbonates become more thermally stable down the group?
o: Larger cations have lower charge density and polarise the carbonate ion less
Lattice energy increases down the group
questions.why: Less distortion of the carbonate's electron cloud means it breaks up less easily.

questions.q: Why does the solubility of the Group 2 sulfates decrease down the group?
o: The lattice energy becomes much more exothermic down the group
The enthalpy change of hydration of M²⁺ becomes less exothermic, while the lattice energy changes much less
Sulfate ions become larger down the group
The sulfates become more covalent down the group
questions.why: The large sulfate ion dominates the lattice, so lattice energy falls only slightly as M²⁺ grows; hydration enthalpy falls more, so ΔHsol becomes more endothermic.

questions.q: What are the products when calcium nitrate is heated strongly?
questions.why: Group 2 nitrates decompose to the oxide, nitrogen dioxide and oxygen: 2Ca(NO₃)₂ → 2CaO + 4NO₂ + O₂. Forming the nitrite and oxygen is typical of Group 1 nitrates.

long.q: Explain why the thermal stability of the Group 2 carbonates increases down the group.
scheme: B1: the cations have the same charge but their radius increases down the group, so charge density decreases
B1: a small Mg²⁺ ion polarises (distorts) the electron cloud of the carbonate ion more than a large Ba²⁺ ion
B1: polarisation weakens the C–O bonds in the carbonate ion, so CO₂ is released more easily
B1: so MgCO₃ decomposes at the lowest temperature and BaCO₃ needs the highest

long.q: Use the enthalpy changes involved to explain why the solubility of the Group 2 sulfates decreases down the group.
scheme: B1: ΔHsol = ΔHhyd(cation) + ΔHhyd(anion) − ΔHlatt
B1: down the group the cation gets larger, so both the lattice energy and the hydration enthalpy of the cation become less exothermic
B1: the sulfate ion is large, so the lattice energy changes only slightly as the cation gets bigger
B1: the hydration enthalpy of the cation becomes much less exothermic
B1: so ΔHsol becomes more endothermic (less exothermic) and solubility decreases

long.q: Write an equation for the thermal decomposition of magnesium nitrate and describe what you would see. Explain whether magnesium nitrate or barium nitrate decomposes at the lower temperature. Calculate the total volume of gas, at room conditions, produced by complete decomposition of 0.0100 mol of magnesium nitrate (molar gas volume 24.0 dm³ mol⁻¹).
scheme: B1: 2Mg(NO₃)₂ → 2MgO + 4NO₂ + O₂
B1: brown fumes (NO₂) are given off and a white solid remains
B1: magnesium nitrate, because the smaller Mg²⁺ ion has a higher charge density and polarises the nitrate ion more
M1: 1 mol Mg(NO₃)₂ gives 2.5 mol gas, so 0.0100 mol gives 0.0250 mol

long.q: The hydration enthalpies of Mg²⁺ and Ba²⁺ are −1920 and −1360 kJ mol⁻¹. Explain this difference, and explain why the Group 2 hydroxides become more soluble down the group.
scheme: B1: Mg²⁺ is smaller than Ba²⁺ with the same charge, so it has a higher charge density
B1: it attracts the δ− oxygen atoms of water molecules more strongly (stronger ion–dipole attraction)
B1: OH⁻ is a small ion, so the lattice energy of the hydroxides becomes much less exothermic as the cation gets bigger, faster than the hydration enthalpy falls
B1: so ΔHsol becomes more exothermic (less endothermic) down the group, and solubility increases

long.q: The lattice energy of strontium chloride is −2156 kJ mol⁻¹. The enthalpy changes of hydration are Sr²⁺ −1480 and Cl⁻ −364 kJ mol⁻¹. Calculate the enthalpy change of solution of strontium chloride, and state, with a reason, whether the hydration enthalpy of Ca²⁺ is more or less exothermic than that of Sr²⁺.
scheme: M1: ΔHsol = ΔHhyd(Sr²⁺) + 2ΔHhyd(Cl⁻) − ΔHlatt
M1: sum of hydration enthalpies = −1480 + 2(−364) = −2208 kJ mol⁻¹
A1: ΔHsol = −2208 + 2156 = −52 kJ mol⁻¹
B1: more exothermic, because Ca²⁺ is smaller (higher charge density) and attracts water molecules more strongly

questions.q: Why are transition metal compounds often coloured?
o: d-orbitals split in a ligand field and electrons absorb visible light moving between them
questions.why: The light not absorbed gives the complementary colour.

questions.q: What is the coordination number of [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺?
questions.why: Six water ligands form dative bonds to Cu²⁺.

questions.q: Which is a bidentate ligand?
questions.why: en forms two dative bonds through its two nitrogen atoms.

questions.q: Why do transition metal complexes exhibit distinct colours in aqueous solution?
o: d-orbitals split in energy and d-electrons absorb specific frequencies of visible light
Transitions occur between s and p orbitals
Electrons emit light during nuclear decay
questions.why: Ligand field splitting causes d-d electronic transitions; the absorbed photons promote electrons, leaving the complementary colour visible.

questions.q: Concentrated HCl is added to pink aqueous cobalt(II) ions: [Co(H₂O)₆]²⁺ + 4Cl⁻ ⇌ [CoCl₄]²⁻ + 6H₂O. Which describes the change?
o: Blue to pink; the coordination number stays at 6
Pink to blue; octahedral (6-coordinate) to tetrahedral (4-coordinate)
Pink to blue; the oxidation state of cobalt changes from +2 to +4
Pink to green; octahedral to square planar
questions.why: This is ligand exchange: the larger Cl⁻ ligands replace water, and only four fit around Co²⁺, giving a blue tetrahedral complex. Cobalt stays +2 (6 × 0 → 4 × −1 with overall charge 2+ → 2−).

long.q: Explain why aqueous copper(II) ions are coloured.
scheme: B1: ligands split the 3d orbitals into two energy levels
B1: a d electron absorbs light of a particular frequency to move to the higher level
B1: the complementary colour is seen (blue)
B1: Cu²⁺ has a partly filled 3d subshell (3d⁹)

long.q: Define a transition element, and explain why zinc is not a transition element although it is in the d block. Explain why transition elements show variable oxidation states, giving an example.
scheme: B1: a d-block element that forms one or more stable ions with an incomplete d subshell
B1: zinc forms only Zn²⁺, which has a full 3d¹⁰ subshell
B1: the 3d and 4s electrons are close in energy, so different numbers of them can be lost or used in bonding
B1: e.g. iron forms +2 and +3, or manganese forms +2, +4 and +7

long.q: Excess concentrated hydrochloric acid is added to aqueous copper(II) sulfate. Describe the colour change, write an equation, and give the shape and coordination number of the copper complex before and after.
scheme: B1: the blue solution turns yellow (yellow-green)
B1: [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ + 4Cl⁻ ⇌ [CuCl₄]²⁻ + 6H₂O (ligand exchange)
B1: [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ is octahedral, coordination number 6
B1: [CuCl₄]²⁻ is tetrahedral, coordination number 4
B1: the change happens because Cl⁻ ligands are larger than water molecules, so only four fit around Cu²⁺

long.q: An iron tablet of mass 2.50 g is dissolved in dilute sulfuric acid and made up to 250 cm³. A 25.0 cm³ portion needs 18.40 cm³ of 0.0100 mol dm⁻³ potassium manganate(VII) to react with the Fe²⁺ ions. MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5Fe²⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 5Fe³⁺ + 4H₂O. Calculate the percentage by mass of iron in the tablet (Ar Fe = 55.8), and explain why no indicator is needed.
scheme: B1: MnO₄⁻ is purple and Mn²⁺ almost colourless, so the end-point is the first permanent pale pink colour

long.q: Describe the stereoisomerism shown by Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂ and by [Ni(H₂NCH₂CH₂NH₂)₃]²⁺, stating the shape of each complex and the type of isomerism.
scheme: B1: Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂ is square planar
B1: it has cis and trans (geometrical) isomers: the Cl ligands at 90° in cis, at 180° in trans (cis-platin is the anticancer drug)
B1: [Ni(en)₃]²⁺ is octahedral, with three bidentate ligands
B1: it shows optical isomerism: two non-superimposable mirror-image forms

topics.name: Introduction to A Level organic chemistry

questions.q: Benzene's bond lengths are all equal because…
o: its π electrons are delocalised over the ring
questions.why: Delocalisation gives six identical C–C bonds between single and double.

questions.q: Molecules that are non-superimposable mirror images show which isomerism?
questions.why: They rotate plane-polarised light in opposite directions.

questions.q: A chiral centre is a carbon atom that is:
o: bonded to four different atoms or groups
part of a C=C double bond
questions.why: Four different groups make two mirror-image arrangements possible.

questions.q: Which of these compounds contains a chiral centre?
questions.why: C-2 of 2-hydroxypropanoic acid carries four different groups (CH₃, H, OH, COOH). In propan-2-ol the central carbon has two identical CH₃ groups.

questions.q: A chemist makes a chiral compound as a racemic mixture. How does this sample affect plane-polarised light?
o: No net rotation, because equal amounts of each enantiomer rotate the plane equally in opposite directions
questions.why: A racemic mixture contains 50% of each enantiomer; their opposite rotations cancel, so the mixture is optically inactive.

long.q: Describe the bonding in a benzene molecule, including the hybridisation of the carbon atoms, the shape of the molecule, and the evidence that all the carbon–carbon bonds are the same.
scheme: B1: each carbon is sp² hybridised and forms σ bonds to two carbons and one hydrogen
B1: the molecule is a planar hexagon with bond angles of 120°
B1: each carbon has one unhybridised p orbital, which overlaps sideways with the p orbitals on both neighbouring carbons
B1: this gives a ring of delocalised π electrons above and below the plane of the ring
B1: all C–C bond lengths are equal (0.139 nm), between those of C–C and C=C

long.q: Threonine is CH₃CH(OH)CH(NH₂)COOH. Identify each chiral centre and state the maximum number of stereoisomers of threonine.
scheme: B1: carbon 2 (bonded to H, NH₂, COOH and CH(OH)CH₃)
B1: carbon 3 (bonded to H, OH, CH₃ and CH(NH₂)COOH)
B1: two chiral centres, so 2² = 4 stereoisomers

long.q: Explain why the laboratory synthesis of a chiral drug often produces a racemic mixture, and why drug companies try to make only one enantiomer.
scheme: B1: many reactions go through a planar intermediate (e.g. a C=O group or carbocation), which a reagent attacks from either side with equal probability
B1: so the two enantiomers form in equal amounts: a racemic mixture, which has no overall effect on plane-polarised light
B1: often only one enantiomer has the desired effect (fits the target receptor); the other may be inactive or cause side effects
B1: a single enantiomer allows a smaller dose and fewer side effects (made using enzymes, chiral catalysts or by separating the isomers)

long.q: Name each compound: C₆H₅COCl; CH₃CONH₂; C₆H₅NH₂; CH₃CH₂COOC₆H₅; C₆H₅CH₂OH.
scheme: B1: benzoyl chloride
B1: ethanamide
B1: phenylamine
B1: phenyl propanoate
B1: phenylmethanol

long.q: Give the hybridisation of each carbon atom and the bond angle around it in propanenitrile, CH₃CH₂CN, and describe the bonding in the C≡N group. Compare with the carbonyl carbon of propanal.
scheme: B1: the CH₃ and CH₂ carbons are sp³, tetrahedral, 109.5°
B1: the nitrile carbon is sp, linear, 180°
B1: C≡N is one σ bond and two π bonds
B1: the carbonyl carbon of propanal is sp², trigonal planar, 120°

questions.q: Benzene reacts with bromine in the presence of FeBr₃ by…
questions.why: Substitution keeps the stable delocalised ring.

questions.q: What is the electrophile in the nitration of benzene?
questions.why: Concentrated HNO₃ and H₂SO₄ form the nitronium ion NO₂⁺.

questions.q: How does benzene react with bromine in the presence of FeBr₃?
questions.why: Substitution keeps the stable delocalised ring; FeBr₃ makes the Br⁺ electrophile.

questions.q: Methylbenzene is heated under reflux with alkaline KMnO₄, then the mixture is acidified. What is the organic product?
questions.why: Hot KMnO₄ oxidises the alkyl side chain to –COOH while the stable aromatic ring is left intact.

questions.q: Methylbenzene reacts with chlorine in UV light with no catalyst. Where does substitution happen?
o: On the ring, mainly at the 2- and 4-positions
Chlorine atoms add across the ring's double bonds
Nowhere: no reaction occurs without a halogen carrier
On the methyl group, by free-radical substitution, giving C₆H₅CH₂Cl
questions.why: UV light produces Cl• radicals, which substitute H atoms on the alkyl side chain. Ring substitution at the 2- and 4-positions needs a halogen carrier such as AlCl₃.

long.q: Explain why benzene undergoes substitution rather than addition with bromine, and name the catalyst used.
scheme: B1: delocalised π electrons give extra stability
B1: substitution keeps the delocalised ring; addition would destroy it
B1: catalyst FeBr₃ (or AlBr₃ / iron)

long.q: Describe the mechanism of the nitration of benzene, including the reagents, conditions and how the electrophile is formed.
scheme: B1: concentrated nitric acid and concentrated sulfuric acid, below 55 °C
B1: HNO₃ + 2H₂SO₄ → NO₂⁺ + H₃O⁺ + 2HSO₄⁻ (or HNO₃ + H₂SO₄ → NO₂⁺ + HSO₄⁻ + H₂O)
B1: the delocalised π electrons attack NO₂⁺, forming a positively charged intermediate in which the delocalisation is partly broken
B1: the intermediate loses H⁺, restoring the delocalised ring and giving nitrobenzene (electrophilic substitution)
B1: H⁺ + HSO₄⁻ → H₂SO₄, so sulfuric acid is regenerated (a catalyst)

long.q: Methylbenzene reacts with chlorine under two sets of conditions: (i) ultraviolet light; (ii) an AlCl₃ catalyst at room temperature in the dark. Name the organic product(s) and the type of reaction in each case. Name the product of heating methylbenzene with alkaline KMnO₄ and then acidifying.
scheme: B1: (i) (chloromethyl)benzene, C₆H₅CH₂Cl
B1: free-radical substitution in the methyl side chain
B1: (ii) 2-chloromethylbenzene and 4-chloromethylbenzene
B1: electrophilic substitution in the ring (the methyl group directs to the 2- and 4-positions)
B1: benzoic acid, C₆H₅COOH

long.q: The enthalpy change of hydrogenation of cyclohexene is −120 kJ mol⁻¹, and that of benzene is −208 kJ mol⁻¹. Explain what these values show about the structure of benzene.
scheme: M1: a structure with three separate C=C bonds would give 3 × (−120) = −360 kJ mol⁻¹
A1: benzene is 360 − 208 = 152 kJ mol⁻¹ more stable than expected
B1: the extra stability comes from the delocalisation of the π electrons around the ring
B1: so benzene does not behave like an alkene (e.g. it does not decolourise bromine water)

long.q: Benzene reacts with chloroethane in the presence of aluminium chloride. Name the organic product and write an equation. Explain the role of aluminium chloride, with equations showing how it forms the electrophile and how it is regenerated.
scheme: B1: ethylbenzene: C₆H₆ + C₂H₅Cl → C₆H₅C₂H₅ + HCl
B1: CH₃CH₂Cl + AlCl₃ → CH₃CH₂⁺ + AlCl₄⁻
B1: AlCl₃ accepts a lone pair from chlorine (it is a halogen carrier / Lewis acid), producing the electrophile CH₃CH₂⁺
B1: H⁺ + AlCl₄⁻ → AlCl₃ + HCl, so the catalyst is regenerated

questions.q: Why is chlorobenzene much less reactive to nucleophiles than chloroalkanes?
o: The C–Cl bond is strengthened by overlap with the ring's π system
questions.why: Partial double-bond character makes the C–Cl bond harder to break.

questions.q: Why is chlorobenzene much less reactive towards nucleophiles than chloroethane?
o: Chlorine is more electronegative in benzene
A chlorine lone pair overlaps with the ring's π system, strengthening the C–Cl bond
questions.why: The partial double-bond character makes the C–Cl bond harder to break.

questions.q: Which halogenoalkane is hydrolysed fastest?
questions.why: The C–I bond is the weakest, so it breaks most easily.

questions.q: Which reagents and conditions convert benzene into chlorobenzene?
o: Cl₂ with an AlCl₃ catalyst at room temperature
questions.why: The halogen carrier AlCl₃ (or FeCl₃) polarises Cl₂ to make the Cl⁺ electrophile for electrophilic substitution; benzene does not react with HCl.

questions.q: Chlorobenzene and 1-chlorobutane are each warmed with aqueous NaOH, then acidified with dilute HNO₃ and aqueous AgNO₃ added. What is seen?
o: A white precipitate only with chlorobenzene
questions.why: Only 1-chlorobutane is hydrolysed to release Cl⁻; the C–Cl bond in chlorobenzene is strengthened by overlap with the ring, so no Cl⁻ forms.

long.q: Explain why chlorobenzene is not hydrolysed by warm aqueous sodium hydroxide, although 1-chlorobutane is hydrolysed under these conditions.
scheme: B1: a lone pair on the chlorine atom overlaps with (is partly delocalised into) the π electron system of the ring
B1: so the C–Cl bond has some double-bond character and is stronger (and shorter) than in a chloroalkane
B1: the electron-rich π cloud of the ring repels an approaching nucleophile such as OH⁻
B1: the ring also blocks attack from the side opposite the chlorine, so SN2 attack cannot happen

long.q: Describe how bromobenzene is made from benzene: give the reagents and conditions, an equation, and equations showing how the catalyst forms the electrophile and is regenerated.
scheme: B1: bromine with an iron(III) bromide catalyst (or iron filings), at room temperature, in the absence of water
B1: C₆H₆ + Br₂ → C₆H₅Br + HBr
B1: Br₂ + FeBr₃ → Br⁺ + FeBr₄⁻
B1: H⁺ + FeBr₄⁻ → FeBr₃ + HBr

long.q: Describe a chemical test to distinguish chlorobenzene, C₆H₅Cl, from (chloromethyl)benzene, C₆H₅CH₂Cl, and explain the difference in behaviour.
scheme: B1: warm each with silver nitrate in aqueous ethanol (or warm with NaOH(aq), acidify with dilute HNO₃, then add AgNO₃(aq))
B1: (chloromethyl)benzene gives a white precipitate of AgCl
B1: chlorobenzene gives no precipitate
B1: in C₆H₅CH₂Cl the Cl is on a side-chain carbon, so it is hydrolysed like a chloroalkane, releasing Cl⁻; in C₆H₅Cl the C–Cl bond is strengthened by overlap with the ring

long.q: Put ethanoyl chloride, 1-chloropropane and chlorobenzene in order of ease of hydrolysis, describe the conditions each needs, and explain the order.
scheme: B1: ethanoyl chloride > 1-chloropropane > chlorobenzene
B1: ethanoyl chloride reacts vigorously with cold water, giving steamy fumes of HCl
B1: its carbonyl carbon is bonded to both O and Cl, so it is strongly δ+ and readily attacked by water
B1: 1-chloropropane needs heating with aqueous NaOH (slow)
B1: chlorobenzene is not hydrolysed under normal conditions, because its C–Cl bond is strengthened by overlap of a Cl lone pair with the ring

long.q: The mass spectrum of chlorobenzene shows molecular ion peaks at m/z = 112 and 114 and a large peak at m/z = 77. Explain these peaks, give the ratio of the heights of the 112 and 114 peaks, and state the pattern of molecular ion peaks you would expect for a dichlorobenzene.
scheme: B1: 112 is C₆H₅³⁵Cl⁺ and 114 is C₆H₅³⁷Cl⁺
B1: ratio 3 : 1, the natural ratio of ³⁵Cl to ³⁷Cl
B1: 77 is C₆H₅⁺, formed by loss of a chlorine atom
B1: a dichlorobenzene gives M, M+2 and M+4 peaks (146, 148, 150) in the ratio 9 : 6 : 1

questions.q: Phenol reacts with bromine water to give…
questions.why: The OH group activates the ring, so substitution happens readily without a catalyst.

questions.q: Which is the strongest acid?
questions.why: Order: ethanoic acid > phenol > water > ethanol.

questions.q: Why is phenol more acidic than ethanol?
o: The phenoxide ion's negative charge is delocalised into the ring
questions.why: A more stable anion means the O–H proton is lost more readily.

questions.q: Which of these does phenol react with: sodium metal, aqueous NaOH, aqueous Na₂CO₃?
questions.why: Phenol is acidic enough to react with Na and NaOH, but it is too weak an acid to release CO₂ from carbonate, unlike carboxylic acids.

questions.q: Why does phenol react with bromine water at room temperature with no catalyst, while benzene needs a halogen carrier?
o: Phenol is a stronger acid than benzene
The OH group makes phenol more soluble in water
Bromine water is a stronger electrophile than Br₂ alone
A lone pair on the oxygen is delocalised into the ring, raising its electron density so it attacks the electrophile more readily
questions.why: The increased electron density of the ring in phenol can polarise Br₂ itself, so substitution (at the 2-, 4- and 6-positions) happens readily without a catalyst.

long.q: Put ethanol, phenol and water in order of increasing acidity, and explain the order in terms of the stability of the anions formed. Give one reaction that shows phenol is more acidic than ethanol.
scheme: B1: ethanol < water < phenol
B1: in the phenoxide ion the negative charge on oxygen is delocalised into the benzene ring (overlap with the π system)
B1: this stabilises the phenoxide ion, so phenol releases H⁺ more readily than water
B1: in the ethoxide ion the electron-donating ethyl group concentrates the negative charge on oxygen, so it is less stable than OH⁻
B1: phenol reacts with (dissolves in) aqueous sodium hydroxide; ethanol does not

long.q: Bromine water is added to aqueous phenol. Describe what you would see, write an equation and name the product. Explain why phenol reacts much more readily with bromine than benzene does.
scheme: B1: the bromine water is decolourised (orange to colourless) and a white precipitate forms
B1: C₆H₅OH + 3Br₂ → C₆H₂Br₃OH + 3HBr; 2,4,6-tribromophenol
B1: a lone pair on the oxygen is delocalised into the ring, increasing its electron density
B1: so the ring is activated and attacks the electrophile without a catalyst at room temperature; benzene needs Br₂ with a FeBr₃ catalyst

long.q: Compare the conditions needed for the nitration of phenol and of benzene, naming the products formed from phenol and explaining the difference.
scheme: B1: phenol: dilute nitric acid at room temperature
B1: products 2-nitrophenol and 4-nitrophenol
B1: benzene: concentrated nitric acid with concentrated sulfuric acid at about 50 °C
B1: the –OH group activates the ring (by donating electron density) and directs substitution to the 2- and 4-positions

long.q: Outline how phenol can be made from phenylamine, giving reagents, conditions and equations, and explain why the temperature must be controlled in the first stage.
scheme: B1: phenylamine with sodium nitrite and dilute hydrochloric acid (nitrous acid made in the mixture)
B1: below 10 °C, forming benzenediazonium chloride, C₆H₅N₂⁺Cl⁻ (above 10 °C it decomposes as it forms)
B1: then warm the diazonium salt solution with water
B1: C₆H₅N₂⁺ + H₂O → C₆H₅OH + N₂ + H⁺

long.q: 0.940 g of phenol is dissolved in water. Write an equation for its reaction with sodium hydroxide and calculate the volume of 0.500 mol dm⁻³ NaOH needed to react with it. Write an equation for the reaction of phenol with sodium and calculate the volume of hydrogen formed from 0.940 g of phenol at room conditions (24.0 dm³ mol⁻¹). (Mr phenol = 94.0)
scheme: B1: C₆H₅OH + NaOH → C₆H₅ONa + H₂O (sodium phenoxide)
B1: 2C₆H₅OH + 2Na → 2C₆H₅ONa + H₂

questions.q: Acyl chlorides react with water to give…
questions.why: Vigorous hydrolysis with steamy HCl fumes.

questions.q: What forms when ethanoyl chloride reacts with water?
questions.why: Acyl chlorides hydrolyse rapidly at room temperature, giving steamy HCl fumes.

questions.q: Which is the strongest acid?
questions.why: Electron-withdrawing chlorine atoms stabilise the carboxylate ion.

questions.q: Ethanoyl chloride reacts with ethylamine. What is the organic product?
questions.why: In nucleophilic addition–elimination, the amine's lone pair attacks the carbonyl carbon and HCl is lost, giving a substituted (N-ethyl) amide.

questions.q: Why is ethanoyl chloride, not ethanoic acid, used to make the ester phenyl ethanoate from phenol?
o: Ethanoic acid is too strong an acid
Phenol reacts with ethanoic acid to give a salt instead
Phenol is a poor nucleophile, so it reacts with the more reactive acyl chloride but not readily with a carboxylic acid
Ethanoyl chloride acts as a catalyst
questions.why: The phenol O lone pair is partly delocalised into the ring, making phenol a weak nucleophile; the carbonyl carbon of an acyl chloride, bonded to both O and Cl, is much more δ+ than in a carboxylic acid.

long.q: Put ethanoic acid, chloroethanoic acid and trichloroethanoic acid in order of increasing acid strength, and explain the order.
scheme: B1: ethanoic < chloroethanoic < trichloroethanoic
B1: chlorine is highly electronegative and withdraws electron density from the carboxyl group
B1: this spreads (delocalises) the negative charge of the carboxylate ion, stabilising it, and weakens the O–H bond
B1: more chlorine atoms give a greater effect, so a larger Ka

long.q: Give two different reagents that convert ethanoic acid into ethanoyl chloride, and an equation for one of them. Describe what you would see when ethanoyl chloride is added to water, and write the equation.
scheme: B1: phosphorus(V) chloride, PCl₅, at room temperature
B1: a second reagent: PCl₃ with heat, or sulfur dichloride oxide, SOCl₂
B1: CH₃COOH + PCl₅ → CH₃COCl + POCl₃ + HCl (or CH₃COOH + SOCl₂ → CH₃COCl + SO₂ + HCl)
B1: a vigorous reaction at room temperature with steamy white fumes (HCl)
B1: CH₃COCl + H₂O → CH₃COOH + HCl

long.q: Describe the mechanism of the reaction between ethanoyl chloride and ethanol, name the organic product, and give one advantage of using ethanoyl chloride instead of ethanoic acid to make this product.
scheme: B1: a lone pair on the O of ethanol attacks the δ+ carbonyl carbon (δ+ because it is bonded to both O and Cl)
B1: the C=O π bond breaks, giving a tetrahedral intermediate (addition)
B1: the C=O reforms, Cl⁻ is eliminated and H⁺ is lost, forming HCl (elimination)
B1: ethyl ethanoate; the reaction is fast at room temperature and goes to completion (not an equilibrium), so the yield is higher

long.q: Explain why phenyl ethanoate is not made by heating phenol with ethanoic acid. Give a suitable reagent and an equation for its preparation, and name the products when phenyl ethanoate is heated with excess aqueous sodium hydroxide.
scheme: B1: the lone pair on the oxygen of phenol is delocalised into the ring, so phenol is a poor nucleophile and reacts too slowly with ethanoic acid
B1: use ethanoyl chloride (at room temperature)
B1: CH₃COCl + C₆H₅OH → CH₃COOC₆H₅ + HCl
B1: sodium ethanoate and sodium phenoxide (and water)

long.q: 25.0 cm³ of aqueous ethanedioic acid is warmed and titrated with 0.0200 mol dm⁻³ potassium manganate(VII); 22.50 cm³ is needed. 2MnO₄⁻ + 5H₂C₂O₄ + 6H⁺ → 2Mn²⁺ + 10CO₂ + 8H₂O. Calculate the concentration of the ethanedioic acid. Explain why the solution is warmed, and name the product of oxidising methanoic acid.
scheme: A1: concentration = 1.125 × 10⁻³ ÷ 0.0250 = 0.0450 mol dm⁻³
B1: the reaction is very slow at room temperature (until the Mn²⁺ formed catalyses it), so warming (to about 60 °C) speeds it up
B1: methanoic acid is oxidised to carbon dioxide (and water)

questions.q: Why is phenylamine a weaker base than ethylamine?
o: The lone pair on N is delocalised into the ring, so it's less available
questions.why: Delocalisation reduces the lone pair's ability to accept a proton.

questions.q: Amino acids exist in solution near neutral pH as…
questions.why: The –COOH loses H⁺ and the –NH₂ gains it.

questions.q: Why is phenylamine a weaker base than ammonia?
o: The ring donates electrons to nitrogen
The nitrogen lone pair is partly delocalised into the benzene ring
questions.why: The lone pair is less available to accept a proton.

questions.q: Which reagents and conditions convert phenylamine into benzenediazonium chloride?
o: NaNO₂ and dilute HCl, heated under reflux
Sn and concentrated HCl, then NaOH
questions.why: Nitrous acid is made in situ from NaNO₂ and HCl; the temperature is kept below 10 °C because the diazonium ion decomposes to phenol and N₂ when warmed.

questions.q: In which form does the amino acid glycine mainly exist in a solution of pH 1?
questions.why: In strong acid both groups are protonated: the –NH₂ gains H⁺ and the –COO⁻ of the zwitterion is protonated to –COOH, so the ion carries an overall +1 charge.

long.q: Put ammonia, ethylamine and phenylamine in order of increasing base strength, and explain the order. Write an equation to show ethylamine acting as a base in water.
scheme: B1: phenylamine < ammonia < ethylamine
B1: base strength depends on how available the lone pair on nitrogen is to accept a proton
B1: the ethyl group is electron-donating, increasing the electron density on N
B1: in phenylamine the N lone pair is delocalised into the benzene ring, so it is less available
B1: CH₃CH₂NH₂ + H₂O ⇌ CH₃CH₂NH₃⁺ + OH⁻

long.q: Describe how phenylamine is made from nitrobenzene, giving reagents, conditions and an equation using [H], and explain why sodium hydroxide is added at the end.
scheme: B1: heat nitrobenzene under reflux with tin and concentrated hydrochloric acid
B1: C₆H₅NO₂ + 6[H] → C₆H₅NH₂ + 2H₂O (reduction)
B1: in the acid the product is present as the phenylammonium ion, C₆H₅NH₃⁺
B1: excess NaOH removes H⁺ and releases free phenylamine (which can then be steam distilled)

long.q: Describe how an azo dye can be made from phenylamine and phenol, giving reagents and conditions. Explain why the temperature is controlled in the first step, and identify the feature of the product's structure that makes it coloured.
scheme: B1: phenylamine with sodium nitrite and dilute hydrochloric acid (nitrous acid), below 10 °C
B1: forming the benzenediazonium ion, C₆H₅N₂⁺
B1: above about 10 °C the diazonium ion decomposes (to phenol and nitrogen)
B1: add the cold diazonium solution to phenol dissolved in aqueous NaOH: a yellow-orange precipitate (coupling)
B1: the –N=N– (azo) group links two benzene rings, giving an extended delocalised system that absorbs visible light

long.q: Aminoethanoic acid (glycine) is H₂NCH₂COOH. Give the structure of its zwitterion and explain why glycine has a high melting point. Give the structure of the main species at pH 1 and at pH 12, and state which electrode glycine moves towards during electrophoresis at pH 1.
scheme: B1: zwitterion ⁺H₃NCH₂COO⁻
B1: strong ionic attractions between the charged groups of neighbouring zwitterions need a lot of energy to overcome
B1: pH 1: ⁺H₃NCH₂COOH
B1: pH 12: H₂NCH₂COO⁻
B1: at pH 1 it is positively charged, so it moves towards the cathode (negative electrode)

long.q: Ethanamide can be made from ethanoyl chloride. Write the equation for its formation, give the products of its hydrolysis under acidic and under alkaline conditions, name the product of its reduction by LiAlH₄, and explain why ethanamide is not basic.
scheme: B1: CH₃COCl + 2NH₃ → CH₃CONH₂ + NH₄Cl
B1: heating with dilute HCl gives ethanoic acid and ammonium chloride
B1: heating with aqueous NaOH gives sodium ethanoate and ammonia
B1: LiAlH₄ in dry ether reduces it to ethylamine, CH₃CH₂NH₂
B1: the lone pair on nitrogen is delocalised over the adjacent C=O group, so it is not available to accept a proton

questions.q: A polyester is formed from…
o: a diol and a dicarboxylic acid
questions.why: Ester links form, eliminating water each time (condensation polymerisation).

questions.q: Which pair of monomers forms a polyester?
o: A diol and a dicarboxylic acid
A diamine and a dicarboxylic acid
An amino acid and an alkene
questions.why: Each ester link forms with loss of water; a diamine and a diacid would make a polyamide.

questions.q: Which linkage is found in a polyamide?
questions.why: Nylon and proteins both contain the amide (peptide) link.

questions.q: Nylon-6,6 can be made from hexanedioyl dichloride, ClOC(CH₂)₄COCl, and hexane-1,6-diamine. Which small molecule is eliminated?
questions.why: Each amide link forms from –COCl and –NH₂, losing HCl. Water is lost when the dicarboxylic acid is used instead of the diacyl dichloride.

questions.q: Why can polyesters and polyamides be broken down more easily than poly(alkenes)?
o: They have weaker C–C bonds in the chain
Their ester and amide links can be hydrolysed by acids, alkalis or enzymes
questions.why: Hydrolysis breaks the polar –COO– or –CONH– links back into monomers; poly(alkenes) have only non-polar C–C and C–H bonds and no such reactive link.

long.q: Ethane-1,2-diol and benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid form a polyester. Give its repeat unit, name the linkage and the small molecule eliminated, and state what is eliminated instead if benzene-1,4-dicarbonyl dichloride is used.
scheme: B1: repeat unit –O–CH₂CH₂–O–CO–C₆H₄–CO–
B1: an ester linkage, –COO–
B1: water is eliminated in each condensation step
B1: with the dioyl dichloride, hydrogen chloride is eliminated

long.q: Nylon-6,6 is made from hexane-1,6-diamine and hexanedioic acid. Give its repeat unit, name the linkage formed, and explain why nylon fibres are strong.
scheme: B1: –NH–(CH₂)₆–NH–CO–(CH₂)₄–CO–
B1: an amide linkage, –CONH–
B1: hydrogen bonds form between the N–H of one chain and the C=O of a neighbouring chain
B1: these strong intermolecular forces along the chains give high tensile strength

long.q: Poly(lactic acid) is made from 2-hydroxypropanoic acid, CH₃CH(OH)COOH. Explain how a single monomer can form a condensation polymer, give the repeat unit, and explain why poly(lactic acid) is biodegradable but poly(propene) is not.
scheme: B1: the monomer has both an –OH and a –COOH group, so each molecule can form ester links at both ends
B1: repeat unit –O–CH(CH₃)–CO–
B1: its ester links can be hydrolysed (by water, acids, or enzymes in microorganisms)
B1: poly(propene) has only non-polar C–C and C–H bonds, which are not hydrolysed

long.q: Kevlar has the repeat unit –NH–C₆H₄–NH–CO–C₆H₄–CO– (both rings substituted at the 1,4-positions). Identify the two monomers, give the products of heating Kevlar with hydrochloric acid, and suggest why Kevlar is so strong.
scheme: B1: benzene-1,4-diamine, H₂N–C₆H₄–NH₂
B1: benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid, HOOC–C₆H₄–COOH (or its dioyl dichloride)
B1: acid hydrolysis gives benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid and the diammonium salt ⁺H₃N–C₆H₄–NH₃⁺ 2Cl⁻
B1: rigid, flat chains line up closely and are linked by many hydrogen bonds between N–H and C=O

long.q: State, with a reason, whether each forms an addition or a condensation polymer: (i) CH₂=CHCN; (ii) H₂NCH₂COOH with H₂NCH(CH₃)COOH; (iii) HOCH₂CH₂OH with ClOC(CH₂)₄COCl. Give the structure of one dipeptide formed in (ii) and name its linkage.
scheme: B1: (i) addition: the monomer has a C=C bond and no other product forms
B1: (ii) condensation: amino and carboxyl groups react, eliminating water (forming a polypeptide)
B1: (iii) condensation: a polyester forms, eliminating HCl
B1: H₂NCH₂CONHCH(CH₃)COOH (or H₂NCH(CH₃)CONHCH₂COOH)
B1: a peptide (amide) linkage, –CONH–

questions.q: Which reagent converts a carboxylic acid to an acyl chloride?
questions.why: SOCl₂ (or PCl₅) replaces OH with Cl.

questions.q: How is phenylamine made from benzene?
o: Nitrate with conc. HNO₃ and H₂SO₄, then reduce with Sn and conc. HCl
questions.why: Nitration gives nitrobenzene; reduction gives phenylamine (freed with NaOH).

questions.q: Which reagent converts a carboxylic acid into an acyl chloride?
questions.why: PCl₅ or PCl₃ also work; aqueous HCl does not.

questions.q: Which reagent distinguishes phenol from cyclohexanol?
questions.why: Phenol decolourises bromine water and gives a white precipitate; cyclohexanol does not react. Both react with sodium, and neither reacts with Na₂CO₃ or Tollens' reagent.

questions.q: Propanal reacts with HCN (with KCN catalyst). Why is the product obtained as a racemic mixture?
o: The product has no chiral centre
The C=O group is planar, so CN⁻ attacks from either side with equal probability
questions.why: Attack from the two faces of the planar carbonyl gives the two enantiomers of 2-hydroxybutanenitrile in equal amounts, so a single-enantiomer product would need further separation.

long.q: Suggest a three-step synthesis of N-phenylethanamide, C₆H₅NHCOCH₃, from benzene. Give the reagents and conditions for each step and name each intermediate.
scheme: B1: step 1: concentrated HNO₃ and concentrated H₂SO₄, below 55 °C
B1: intermediate nitrobenzene
B1: step 2: tin and concentrated HCl, heat under reflux, then add NaOH
B1: intermediate phenylamine
B1: step 3: ethanoyl chloride at room temperature: C₆H₅NH₂ + CH₃COCl → C₆H₅NHCOCH₃ + HCl

long.q: Tyrosine is HO–C₆H₄–CH₂CH(NH₂)COOH (the ring is substituted at the 1,4-positions). Name its three functional groups, and predict the organic product of its reaction with: excess bromine water; excess aqueous sodium hydroxide; dilute hydrochloric acid; excess ethanoyl chloride.
scheme: B1: phenol, primary amine and carboxylic acid
B1: bromine water: substitution at both ring positions next to the –OH (the 4-position is already taken), giving a dibromo product and a white precipitate
B1: NaOH: both the phenol –OH and the –COOH lose H⁺, giving ⁻O–C₆H₄–CH₂CH(NH₂)COO⁻
B1: HCl: the amine is protonated, giving HO–C₆H₄–CH₂CH(NH₃⁺)COOH
B1: ethanoyl chloride: the –NH₂ forms an amide and the phenol –OH forms an ester

long.q: Suggest a two-step synthesis of 1-phenylethanol, C₆H₅CH(OH)CH₃, from benzene. Give the reagents and conditions, name the intermediate, and explain why the product is obtained as a racemic mixture.
scheme: B1: step 1: ethanoyl chloride with an anhydrous AlCl₃ catalyst (Friedel–Crafts acylation)
B1: the electrophile is CH₃CO⁺; intermediate phenylethanone, C₆H₅COCH₃
B1: step 2: reduce with NaBH₄ (or LiAlH₄ in dry ether)
B1: the product has a chiral centre (C bonded to H, OH, CH₃ and C₆H₅)
B1: the C=O group is planar, so H⁻ attacks from either side with equal probability, giving equal amounts of both enantiomers

long.q: Give the reagents and conditions for each conversion: (i) methylbenzene to benzoic acid; (ii) benzoic acid to benzoyl chloride; (iii) benzoyl chloride to N-methylbenzamide, C₆H₅CONHCH₃; (iv) benzoic acid to phenylmethanol.
scheme: B1: (i) heat under reflux with alkaline KMnO₄, then acidify with dilute H₂SO₄ (or HCl)
B1: (ii) PCl₅ at room temperature (or SOCl₂)
B1: (iii) methylamine, CH₃NH₂, at room temperature
B1: (iv) LiAlH₄ in dry ether

long.q: Suggest a two-step synthesis of propylamine, CH₃CH₂CH₂NH₂, from bromoethane, with reagents, conditions and an equation for the second step. Explain why this route gives a purer product than heating 1-bromopropane with ammonia.
scheme: B1: step 1: KCN in ethanol, heat under reflux, giving propanenitrile
B1: step 2: reduce with LiAlH₄ in dry ether (or hydrogen with a nickel catalyst)
B1: CH₃CH₂CN + 4[H] → CH₃CH₂CH₂NH₂
B1: the ammonia route gives a mixture of primary, secondary and tertiary amines (and quaternary salts); the nitrile route gives only the primary amine

questions.q: In proton NMR, a peak split into a triplet has how many H on adjacent carbons?
questions.why: The n + 1 rule: n = 2 gives a triplet.

questions.q: Why is D₂O added in proton NMR?
o: To identify O–H and N–H protons, whose peaks disappear
questions.why: Deuterium exchanges with labile protons, removing their peaks.

questions.q: Why is D₂O added to a sample in proton NMR?
o: It is the reference at 0 ppm
O–H and N–H protons exchange with D, so their peaks disappear
questions.why: Comparing spectra with and without D₂O identifies the O–H or N–H peak.

questions.q: In thin-layer chromatography a spot moves 3.0 cm while the solvent front moves 7.5 cm from the baseline. What is the Rf value?
questions.why: Rf = distance moved by the spot ÷ distance moved by the solvent front = 3.0 ÷ 7.5 = 0.40; Rf is always less than 1.

questions.q: How many peaks are in the ¹³C NMR spectrum of propan-2-ol, CH₃CH(OH)CH₃?
questions.why: The two CH₃ carbons are in identical environments, and the CH carbon is different, so there are two carbon environments and two peaks.

long.q: A compound has an ¹H NMR spectrum showing a triplet (3H) at δ 1.2 and a quartet (2H) at δ 3.6, and a broad peak that disappears with D₂O. Identify the compound and explain the splitting.
scheme: B1: ethanol, CH₃CH₂OH
B1: the CH₃ triplet is next to a CH₂ (n + 1 = 3)
B1: the CH₂ quartet is next to a CH₃
B1: the O–H peak disappears as H exchanges with D

long.q: Describe how thin-layer chromatography is used to separate the components of a mixture and explain how the separation works. A spot travels 3.6 cm while the solvent front travels 8.0 cm; calculate its Rf value.
scheme: B1: put a spot of the mixture on a pencil baseline on a plate coated with silica or alumina (the stationary phase)
B1: stand the plate in a little solvent (the mobile phase) below the baseline, in a covered container, until the solvent nears the top
B1: components separate because they differ in how strongly they are adsorbed onto the stationary phase compared with how soluble they are in the mobile phase
M1: Rf = distance moved by the spot ÷ distance moved by the solvent front

long.q: Explain how gas chromatography separates the components of a mixture of volatile liquids, and how the chromatogram is used to find the relative amounts of the components.
scheme: B1: the mobile phase is an unreactive carrier gas (e.g. helium or nitrogen)
B1: the stationary phase is a high-boiling liquid on a solid support inside a long column
B1: each component spends a different time dissolved in the stationary phase, so it has its own retention time
B1: the area under each peak is proportional to the amount of that component, so relative peak areas give the percentage composition

long.q: State the number of peaks in the carbon-13 NMR spectrum of: propan-1-ol; propan-2-ol; propanone; methylbenzene. State which of these compounds gives a peak at about 205 ppm, and why.
scheme: B1: propan-1-ol: 3 peaks
B1: propan-2-ol: 2 peaks
B1: propanone: 2 peaks

long.q: A compound C₄H₈O₂ has a proton NMR spectrum in CDCl₃ showing a singlet (3H) at δ 2.0, a quartet (2H) at δ 4.1 and a triplet (3H) at δ 1.3. Deduce its structure, explaining each signal. Explain why CDCl₃ is used as the solvent and tetramethylsilane is added.
scheme: B1: singlet (3H) at δ 2.0: a CH₃ next to C=O with no H on the adjacent carbon
B1: quartet (2H) at δ 4.1: a CH₂ bonded to oxygen and next to a CH₃ (3 + 1 = 4)
B1: triplet (3H) at δ 1.3: a CH₃ next to a CH₂ (2 + 1 = 3)
B1: ethyl ethanoate, CH₃COOCH₂CH₃
B1: CDCl₃ contains no ¹H atoms, so the solvent gives no peak in the spectrum
